ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 40-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 40 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

OUTPUT — exactly this JSON object, nothing else:
{
  "synthesis_unit": {
    "activity_title": "…",
    "pedagogical_method": "one of: Discovery · Problem-solving · Play-way · Inductive ·
      Deductive — the method this unit runs on",
    "section_goal": "recall | reason | apply — the goal this unit works at",
    "teacher_notes": "a few sentences: how the sitting runs, what to watch for, and the
      chapter method each problem needs — NOT the solutions, which are in the table",
    "visual_aids": [
      {"type": "table",
        "title": "Problems and solutions",
        "table": "No. | Problem | Solution\n1 | … | …\n2 | … | …"}
    ],
    "materials": ["…"],
    "time_bands": [
      {"minutes": "0-N", "activity": "…"},
      …bands in sequence, integer boundaries, last band ends at 40…
    ],
    "textbook_items_in_class": [],
    "homework": []
  }
}
No other keys — the platform carries the unit's number, duration, section coverage and
synthesis marker itself.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

{
  "stage": "middle",
  "subject": "mathematics",
  "grade": "vi",
  "chapter_number": 9,
  "chapter_title": "Symmetry",
  "sections": [
    { "ref": "section 9.1", "title": "Line of Symmetry", "section_goal": ["recall"] },
    { "ref": "section 9.1 — Figures with more than one line of symmetry", "title": "Figures with more than one line of symmetry", "section_goal": ["recall", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry", "title": "Generating shapes having lines of symmetry", "section_goal": ["apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 9.2", "title": "Rotational Symmetry", "section_goal": ["recall", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 9.2 — Symmetries of a circle", "title": "Symmetries of a circle", "section_goal": ["recall"] }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 9.1 defines and identifies the concept of line of symmetry for two-dimensional figures. Opening with a visual context of flowers, butterflies, rangoli, and pinwheels, the section introduces the idea that symmetry involves parts of a figure repeating in a definite pattern. It then demonstrates the core concept through folding: a triangle folded along a dotted line produces two halves that overlap exactly — these are called mirror halves — while a figure of four puzzle pieces folded along a central line does not produce overlapping halves. A line of symmetry is formally defined as a line that cuts a figure into two parts that exactly overlap when folded along that line.\n\nSection 9.1 (Figures with more than one line of symmetry) then applies this definition and reasons that a figure can have multiple lines of symmetry. Students physically fold a square piece of paper in four ways — vertically, horizontally, and along each diagonal — discovering that a square has four lines of symmetry. The section contrasts this with a non-square rectangle, leading students to reason that a rectangle's diagonal is not a line of symmetry. Several other figures with multiple lines of symmetry are presented, reinforcing that symmetry need not be limited to a single axis.\n\nSection 9.1 (Reflection) explains the connection between folding and reflection. When a figure is folded along a line of symmetry, the part on one side is reflected to the other side. The section illustrates this using a labelled square (corners A, B, C, D) and the vertical line of symmetry: folding reflects B and C to the positions of A and D respectively, and vice versa. Students reason about reflection along the diagonal and the horizontal line of symmetry. A figure possessing such a line is said to have reflection symmetry.\n\nSection 9.1 (Generating shapes having lines of symmetry) applies the concept practically through hands-on activities. In the Ink Blot Devils activity, students fold paper, apply ink to one half, press the halves together, and observe that the resulting figure is symmetric about the fold line. In the Paper Folding and Cutting activity, students fold and cut paper along dotted lines to generate symmetric shapes, then identify their lines of symmetry. A more intricate variant uses multiple folds to create decorative cut-out patterns. These activities move students from recognising to producing symmetrical shapes.\n\nSection 9.2 defines and reasons about rotational symmetry, a second fundamental type of symmetry. A paper windmill — which has no line of symmetry — looks exactly the same after a 90° rotation about its centre. The centre of rotation is defined as the fixed point about which rotation occurs, and an angle of rotational symmetry (or angle of symmetry) is defined as any angle through which the figure looks exactly the same. For the windmill, angles of symmetry are 90°, 180°, 270°, and 360°. A square is similarly examined with four angles of symmetry, and corner labels track where they map under each rotation. The section establishes that 360° is always an angle of symmetry. The section then reasons about radial-arm figures: a parallelogram-strip worked example shows it has no rotational symmetry (only 360°). For a figure with four radial arms spaced 90° apart, there are four angles of symmetry. An irregular three-arm figure also lacks rotational symmetry, but if three arms are spaced 120° apart (360° ÷ 3), the figure has three angles: 120°, 240°, 360°. The generalisation is developed that for n equal radial arms, the smallest angle of symmetry is 360°/n and all angles are multiples of this value. Students reason about 5-arm and 6-arm figures, and encounter the non-integer case of 7 arms (51 3/7°). True/False statements confirm: 360° is always an angle of symmetry, and the smallest whole-number angle must be a factor of 360.\n\nSection 9.2 (Symmetries of a circle) identifies the circle as uniquely symmetric: every angle of rotation is an angle of symmetry when rotating about the centre, and every diameter is a line of reflection symmetry. Real-world examples — ceiling fans, flowers, wheels — illustrate rotational symmetry. The chapter's extended Figure it Out set requires students to apply both types of symmetry to regular polygons, the Ashoka Chakra, the Parliament Building, Koch Snowflake sequences, and tile-based creative designs.",

    {
      "id": "A-1",
      "source_section": "section 9.1",
      "book_ref": "Activity: Folding a square — finding all lines of symmetry, section 9.1 p.220",
      "description": "Students take a square piece of paper and fold it four times (vertically, horizontally, along each diagonal) to discover that a square has four lines of symmetry."
    },
    {
      "id": "A-2",
      "source_section": "section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry",
      "book_ref": "Activity: Ink Blot Devils, section 9.1 p.222",
      "description": "Students fold paper in half, spill ink on one half, press halves together, and open to observe the symmetric figure formed, identifying the fold as the line of symmetry."
    },
    {
      "id": "A-3",
      "source_section": "section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry",
      "book_ref": "Activity: Paper Folding and Cutting, section 9.1 p.223",
      "description": "Students fold paper and cut along dotted lines to generate symmetric shapes; a more intricate variant uses multiple folds to create decorative cut-out patterns with identifiable lines of symmetry."
    },
    {
      "id": "A-4",
      "source_section": "section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry",
      "book_ref": "Activity: Punching Game, section 9.1 p.223",
      "description": "Students punch holes at different locations of a folded square sheet to create symmetric patterns, using the fold as the line of symmetry."
    },
    {
      "id": "A-5",
      "source_section": "section 9.2",
      "book_ref": "Activity: Paper cutout rotation — three-arm radial figure, section 9.2 p.233",
      "description": "Students trace and cut out a three-arm radial figure, then rotate the cutout over the original figure to determine its angles of rotation and verify observations about rotational symmetry."
    },
    {
      "id": "A-6",
      "source_section": "section 9.2 — Symmetries of a circle",
      "book_ref": "Activity: Playing with Tiles, section 9.2 p.239",

    }
  ],

  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.

  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.

  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.

  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.

  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

{
  "stage": "middle",
  "subject": "mathematics",
  "grade": "vii",
  "chapter_number": 4,
  "chapter_title": "Expressions Using Letter-Numbers",
  "sections": [
    { "ref": "section 4.1", "title": "The Notion of Letter-Numbers", "section_goal": ["recall", "apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 4.2", "title": "Revisiting Arithmetic Expressions", "section_goal": ["apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 4.3", "title": "Omission of the Multiplication Symbol in Algebraic Expressions", "section_goal": ["recall", "apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 4.4", "title": "Simplification of Algebraic Expressions", "section_goal": ["reason", "apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 4.5", "title": "Pick Patterns and Reveal Relationships", "section_goal": ["reason", "apply"] }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 4.1 defines letter-numbers and algebraic expressions through three worked examples that move from simple to multi-variable relationships. Example 1 introduces the age-relationship s = a + 3, using a table to show how Shabnam's age is computed from Aftab's for several values, and establishes the vocabulary of 'letter-number' and 'algebraic expression'. Example 2 derives the expression 2n for the number of matchsticks needed to make n L-shapes, showing how a general formula replaces repeated specific calculations. Example 3 extends to a two-variable expression c × 35 + j × 60 for Ketaki's coconut-jaggery cost, explicitly naming the expression a 'formula'. Example 4 uses the perimeter of a square to introduce 4 × q, and the section closes with the Figure it Out exercise where students write perimeter formulas for regular polygons, a combined pipe length, a denomination-count total, a flour-mill timing formula, five English-to-expression translations, and a 2 × 3 calendar-grid cell expression.\n\nSection 4.2 applies the rules for arithmetic expressions — swapping, grouping, bracket removal, and the distributive property — to evaluate seven given numerical expressions. This is explicitly framed as revision of concepts from Chapter 2. The section works through 23 – 10 × 2 (identifying the negative-product term), 83 + 28 – 13 + 32 (swap-and-group), and 68 – (18 + 13) in two ways (bracket-first and distribute-the-negative). Students are asked to evaluate the remaining four expressions using the same methods, and the section bridges to algebraic expressions by noting that they take numerical values when letter-numbers are replaced by numbers.\n\nSection 4.3 defines the shorthand 4n for 4 × n, explains that numbers are written before letters, and applies the convention through the sequence 4, 8, 12, 16, … whose nth term is 4n. The section then asks students to evaluate 7k when k = 4, and 5m + 3 when m = 2, before presenting the 'Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake' exercise: nine numbered algebraic substitutions are shown, some with errors (e.g. reading 10 – a as 6 when a = –4, reading 3d as 36 when d = 6 by confusing concatenation with multiplication), and students must identify, explain, and correct each.\n\nSection 4.4 reasons through the simplification of algebraic expressions using like-term collection and the distributive property, then applies the rules to worked problems. The rectangle perimeter derivation (p = l + b + l + b = 2l + 2b) is the entry point, establishing that two expressions are equal when they yield identical values for all substitutions. Example 5 shows that 5c + 3c + 10c simplifies to 18c via the distributive property, and Example 6 proves 4v + 3v = 7v (and 12n – 4n = 8n) using the area-of-split-rectangle diagram. Like terms and unlike terms are defined. Examples 7–10 escalate to multi-variable bracket removal (chair-table rental: (40x + 75y) – (6x + 10y) = 34x + 65y), quiz-score summation across three rounds, distributive expansion of 4(x + y) – y, and checking whether 5u equals 5 + u. The Figure it Out exercise includes three grid-sum addition tasks, fifteen simplification sub-parts, and eleven 'Mind the Mistake' corrections.\n\nSection 4.5 reasons about general algebraic relationships through pattern-finding, then applies expressions to verify that patterns always hold. The 'Formula Detective' sub-section presents number-machine diagrams where students must reverse-engineer the formula from input-output pairs and write expressions for general inputs. The saree-border pattern example derives 3n – 2, 3n – 1, and 3n as position formulas for designs A, B, C respectively, and uses division-by-3 remainder to identify which design occupies any given position. The calendar 2 × 2 square diagonals are shown to always sum to 2a + 8 by expressing all four entries in terms of the top-left value a and simplifying — a proof by algebraic modelling. The 5-cell cross-shape calendar sum is shown (via Math Talk) to always equal 5 times the centre. Matchstick triangle patterns derive 2y + 1 by two routes (step-count analysis and orientation-split analysis) and confirm they are equal by simplifying 3 + 2(y – 1). The final Figure it Out exercise contains fifteen problems covering expression selection, flag-count reasoning, snail-well expression, Radha's cycling total, expression-path diagrams, a train-timing expression, six simplification problems, six addition problems, six subtraction problems, situation descriptions, rope-cutting pattern, square-matchstick pattern, traffic-signal colour positions, step-sequence square count, and a 4-column number-grid analysis.",
  "enumerated_activities": [],
  "enumerated_worked_examples": [
    {
      "id": "WE-1",
      "source_section": "section 4.1",
      "book_ref": "Example 1, section 4.1 p.81",
      "description": "Shabnam is 3 years older than Aftab. Derive the expression s = a + 3 for Shabnam's age from Aftab's; use it to find Shabnam's age when Aftab is 23."
    },
    {
      "id": "WE-2",
      "source_section": "section 4.1",
      "book_ref": "Example 2, section 4.1 p.82",
      "description": "Parthiv's L-shaped matchstick pattern: derive the expression 2n for the number of matchsticks needed to make n L-shapes."
    },
    {
      "id": "WE-3",
      "source_section": "section 4.1",
      "book_ref": "Example 3, section 4.1 p.82",
      "description": "Ketaki's coconut-jaggery cost: derive the two-variable expression c × 35 + j × 60 and use it to compute cost for 7 coconuts and 4 kg jaggery."
    },
    {
      "id": "WE-4",
      "source_section": "section 4.1",
      "book_ref": "Example 4, section 4.1 p.83",
      "description": "Perimeter of a square as the formula 4 × q; use it to find the perimeter when sidelength is 7 cm."
    },
    {
      "id": "WE-5",
      "source_section": "section 4.4",
      "book_ref": "Example 5, section 4.4 p.88",
      "description": "Pencil-eraser shop over three days: simplify 5c + 3c + 10c = 18c using the distributive property; set up 18c + 11d for total earnings."
    },
    {
      "id": "WE-6",
      "source_section": "section 4.4",
      "book_ref": "Example 6, section 4.4 p.89",
      "description": "Big rectangle split into two smaller rectangles: show 4v + 3v = 7v and 12n – 4n = 8n using two methods of computing area."
    },
    {
      "id": "WE-7",
      "source_section": "section 4.4",
      "book_ref": "Example 7, section 4.4 p.90",
      "description": "Chair-table rental shop: simplify (40x + 75y) – (6x + 10y) to 34x + 65y by distributing the negative sign and collecting like terms."
    },
    {
      "id": "WE-8",
      "source_section": "section 4.4",
      "book_ref": "Example 8, section 4.4 p.91",
      "description": "Charu's three-round quiz scores 7p – 3q, 8p – 4q, 6p – 2q: add to get total 21p – 9q; compare with Krishita's 23p – 7q by finding their difference."
    },

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 40-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 40 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

OUTPUT — exactly this JSON object, nothing else:
{
  "synthesis_unit": {
    "activity_title": "…",
    "pedagogical_method": "one of: Discovery · Problem-solving · Play-way · Inductive ·
      Deductive — the method this unit runs on",

    "teacher_notes": "a few sentences: how the sitting runs, what to watch for, and the
      chapter method each problem needs — NOT the solutions, which are in the table",
    "visual_aids": [
      {"type": "table",
        "title": "Problems and solutions",
        "table": "No. | Problem | Solution\n1 | … | …\n2 | … | …"}
    ],
    "materials": ["…"],
    "time_bands": [
      {"minutes": "0-N", "activity": "…"},
      …bands in sequence, integer boundaries, last band ends at 40…
    ],

  }
}

synthesis marker itself.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

{
  "stage": "middle",
  "subject": "mathematics",
  "grade": "vii",
  "chapter_number": 5,
  "chapter_title": "Parallel and Intersecting Lines",
  "sections": [
    { "ref": "section 5.1", "title": "Across the Line", "section_goal": ["recall", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 5.2", "title": "Perpendicular Lines", "section_goal": ["recall"] },
    { "ref": "section 5.3", "title": "Between Lines", "section_goal": ["recall"] },
    { "ref": "section 5.4", "title": "Parallel and Perpendicular Lines in Paper Folding", "section_goal": ["apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 5.5", "title": "Transversals", "section_goal": ["recall", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 5.6", "title": "Corresponding Angles", "section_goal": ["reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 5.7", "title": "Drawing Parallel Lines", "section_goal": ["apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 5.8", "title": "Alternate Angles", "section_goal": ["reason", "apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 5.9", "title": "Parallel Illusions", "section_goal": ["recall"] }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 5.1 identifies intersecting lines and then reasons about the angle relationships they produce. The section opens by introducing the concept of intersection — two lines meeting at a point on a plane surface form exactly four angles — and immediately progresses to a proof-like reasoning arc: since ∠a + ∠b = 180° and ∠a + ∠d = 180°, it follows that ∠b = ∠d; similarly ∠a = ∠c. This justification is explicitly named a proof in mathematics. Activity 1 is embedded here: students draw four pairs of intersecting lines and measure the resulting angles with a protractor, then reason whether the pattern holds for any measure of ∠a. Adjacent angles at an intersection are defined as linear pairs (always summing to 180°), and opposite angles as vertically opposite angles (always equal). A 'Measurements and Geometry' interlude explains why measured values may deviate from theoretical ones — thickness of drawn lines, protractor error — distinguishing empirical measurement from geometric reasoning.\n\nSection 5.2 defines perpendicular lines as the special case of intersection where all four angles are equal, each measuring 90°. This is a short definitional section that names the concept, states the angle condition, and establishes the standard notation (small square at the intersection).\n\nSection 5.3 identifies parallel lines through observation of real-world examples and a geometric figure. An exploratory task (Fig. 5.5) asks students to describe how various labelled line segments meet, using precise vocabulary (a point, an endpoint, the midpoint, intersect). The formal definition follows: parallel lines lie on the same plane and never meet however far they are extended. A teacher note clarifies that coplanarity is essential — lines on different surfaces may never meet but are not parallel. Students then identify parallel pairs in a dot-grid figure (Fig. 5.6).\n\nSection 5.4 applies the definitions of parallel and perpendicular lines through two hands-on paper-folding activities. Activity 2 guides students to fold a square sheet horizontally in half repeatedly: one fold yields 3 parallel lines, two folds yield 5, three folds yield 9 — revealing a pattern of 2ⁿ + 1 after n folds. A vertical fold creates a new line perpendicular to all previous horizontal folds. A diagonal fold introduces the question of whether the resulting crease has a parallel counterpart. Activity 3 (Fig. 5.8) has students fold corner triangles and reason whether the resulting crease lines a, b, c are parallel to p, q, r respectively. Standard notations are introduced: single/double arrow marks for parallel lines, a square symbol for perpendicular.\n\nSection 5.5 identifies transversals and then reasons about the maximum number of distinct angle measures they create. A transversal is defined as a line that intersects two other lines, forming 8 angles in total. Since vertically opposite angle pairs (∠1 = ∠3, ∠2 = ∠4, ∠5 = ∠7, ∠6 = ∠8) must be equal, the maximum number of distinct angle values is 4. In-text questions prompt students to verify that neither 8 nor 5 distinct measures are possible.\n\nSection 5.6 reasons about corresponding angles and proves that their equality is both necessary and sufficient for the two lines to be parallel. Corresponding angles are defined by their positional correspondence in each set of four angles formed at the two intersection points. Activity 3 constructs a transversal on a given line l so that corresponding angles equal 60°, then draws line m through a second point on the transversal at the same angle — showing that l and m appear parallel. Activity 4 uses tracing paper to verify that corresponding angles on a given pair of parallel lines are equal. Activity 5 shows that drawing a transversal producing equal corresponding angles on non-parallel lines is impossible. The biconditional is thus established: corresponding angles equal if and only if the lines are parallel.\n\nSection 5.7 applies the corresponding-angles criterion to construct parallel lines using two methods. The set square method draws two lines each perpendicular to a baseline l by sliding the set square; since l acts as their transversal with corresponding angles of 90°, the two new lines are parallel. The paper-folding method creates line t perpendicular to l through point A, then creates line m perpendicular to t through A again; since l and m are both perpendicular to t, their corresponding angles with t are both 90° and they are parallel. A Figure it Out question asks students to describe the set square construction in their own words.\n\nSection 5.8 proves that alternate angles are equal when a transversal crosses parallel lines, then applies this result alongside corresponding angles and interior angle sum to solve multi-step problems. The proof chains: alternate angle ∠d of ∠f equals the corresponding angle ∠b of ∠f, and ∠b equals the vertically opposite ∠d, so ∠f = ∠d regardless of measurement. Interior angles — same-side angles between the parallel lines — are introduced and shown to sum to 180°. Four worked examples increase in complexity: Example 1 finds all 8 angles from one given angle; Example 2 tests whether two lines are parallel by checking corresponding angles; Example 3 uses interior angle sum to find a missing angle; Example 4 applies both interior and corresponding angle rules in a parallelogram-like figure. ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 40-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 40 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 40 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

  "prose_summary": "Section 7.1 applies compass-and-ruler construction to produce equilateral triangles. The section opens by noting that while a marked ruler alone can construct an equilateral triangle, trial-and-error makes it inefficient. It then recalls from Grade 6 the method of locating a point equidistant from two given points using arcs. The three-step procedure is made explicit: draw base AB (4 cm), swing an arc of radius 4 cm from A, swing a second arc of radius 4 cm from B, and mark C at their intersection. Joining AC and BC completes the triangle. The correctness is explained by the fact that C lies on both arcs so both AC and BC equal 4 cm.\n\nSection 7.2 reasons through when triangle construction from three given sidelengths is possible and when it is not, then applies the triangle inequality as a decision rule. The construction method (two-arc intersection) is generalised from the equilateral case: base = longest side, then arcs of the other two lengths from the two base endpoints. Five construction tasks are given. The section then explores whether all three lengths produce a triangle: attempting 3, 4, 8 cm and 2, 3, 6 cm fails because the arcs do not intersect. This motivates the triangle inequality: each side must be less than the sum of the other two. The tent-tree-pole path metaphor grounds the reasoning — a direct path is always shorter than a roundabout path via a third point. A complete visual proof via circle-intersection cases (circles touch, don't intersect, intersect internally) establishes that triangle inequality is both necessary and sufficient for existence.\n\nSection 7.3 reasons through the angle-sum property of triangles and proves it using the parallel-line construction, then applies it to find third angles and to determine conditions for triangle existence given two sides and an angle or two angles and a side. For two sides and the included angle, construction is a four-step process (base, angle arm, mark point on arm, join). A Math Talk explores whether any included angle produces a triangle (angles ≥ 180° do not). For two angles and the included side, once the base is drawn the two angle arms are constructed from the base vertices and C is their intersection. The key reasoning is: when the two base angles are supplementary (sum = 180°), the arms are parallel and never meet; when their sum exceeds 180°, C does not exist on the same side. The parallel-line proof of the angle sum property (∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°) is presented formally: draw XY ∥ BC through A, identify alternate angles ∠XAB = ∠B and ∠YAC = ∠C, and note that the three angles together form a straight angle at A. Exterior angles are also derived: exterior angle = sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.\n\nSection 7.4 applies the concept of perpendicular distance to define and construct the altitude of a triangle. The altitude from vertex A to side BC is the perpendicular line segment from A to BC (or its extension). The section introduces the set-square-and-ruler method: align the ruler to the base, place the set square on the ruler, slide until its vertical edge touches the vertex, then draw the altitude. The paper-folding activity (crease from a vertex perpendicular to the base) is embedded as a hands-on verification. The section notes that in a right-angled triangle, one side is itself an altitude, and defines right-angled triangles accordingly.\n\nSection 7.5 identifies and defines the complete classification of triangles. By sides: equilateral (all equal), isosceles (two equal), scalene (all different). By angles: acute-angled (all angles acute), right-angled (one right angle), obtuse-angled (one obtuse angle). The section notes that the two-classification systems are not independent (an equilateral triangle is also acute-angled) but defers full exploration of the relationship to a later chapter. It closes with construction exercises that combine altitude construction with the triangle types, and a Try This on right-angled triangles given only the hypotenuse.",

  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

{
  "stage": "middle",
  "subject": "mathematics",
  "grade": "vii",
  "chapter_number": 9,
  "chapter_title": "Geometric Twins",
  "sections": [
    { "ref": "section 9.1", "title": "Geometric Twins", "section_goal": ["recall", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 9.2", "title": "Congruence of Triangles", "section_goal": ["reason", "apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 9.3", "title": "Angles of Isosceles and Equilateral Triangles", "section_goal": ["reason"] }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 9.1 defines congruence and then reasons about which measurements are enough to recreate a figure exactly. It opens with the practical problem of recreating a signboard symbol on another board: tracing the outline on tracing paper works for small figures but is impractical for big ones, so the section asks what measurements would let us reproduce the figure. Naming the corner points A, B, C, it shows that the two arm lengths AB and BC alone do not fix the symbol — with AB = 4 cm and BC = 8 cm, several different symbols can be built from the same two lengths because the angle between the arms is free to vary. Adding the included angle ∠ABC = 80° does fix the shape and size, so those three measurements produce an exact replica. From this the section states the central definition: figures that are exact copies of each other, having the same shape and size, are congruent, and congruent figures can be superimposed exactly one over the other. It stresses that while checking for congruence a figure may be rotated or flipped before superimposing, so rotated or flipped pairs can still be congruent. The section then returns to the two-symbol verification question and reasons that if both symbols have the same arm lengths and the same included angle we can be sure they are congruent, whereas equal arm lengths alone are not enough. Its Figure it Out set asks students to check given pairs, circle the pairs that appear congruent, and decide what measurements are needed to reproduce a circle or a rectangle and hence how one would test whether two circles, or two rectangles, are congruent.\n\nSection 9.2 justifies the standard triangle-congruence conditions through construction and reasoning, then applies them to identify and express congruence. Framed by Meera and Rabia needing to replicate a triangular frame too big to trace, it works case by case. Measuring the three sidelengths (40, 60, 80 cm, scaled to 4, 6, 8 cm to fit the page) leads to Rabia's construction — a base segment of one length with arcs of the other two lengths swung from its endpoints — which meets at two points forming ∆ABE and ∆ABF; by tracing, taking cut-outs and superimposing, or observing that AB acts as a line of symmetry, these are shown congruent, establishing that equal sidelengths guarantee congruence: the SSS (Side Side Side) condition. The section then develops the conventions for writing congruence (∆ABC ≅ ∆XYZ), explaining that the order of vertices in the two names encodes the corresponding vertices, sides, and angles, so ∆ACB ≅ ∆XYZ would be incorrect while ∆ACB ≅ ∆XZY is a valid restatement; a rectangle split by a diagonal is used to practise finding the correct correspondence via the common side. It next examines the angle-only case (30°, 70°, 80°), showing that equal angles give the same shape but not the same size, so AAA does not guarantee congruence. Two sides and the included angle give the SAS condition, which does guarantee congruence, while two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) are shown by a two-arc construction to permit two non-congruent triangles ∆PQR and ∆PQS — so SSA fails in general. Two angles and the included side give the ASA condition (congruence guaranteed), illustrated further by a figure in which O is the midpoint of AD and BC, where the vertically opposite angles complete an SAS argument. Two angles and a non-included side are reduced to ASA using the fact that a triangle's angles sum to 180° to recover the third angle, giving the AAS condition. Finally, for right triangles, equal hypotenuse and one leg give the RHS condition, a special case in which SSA does guarantee congruence, shown by a perpendicular-and-arc construction. The section closes by listing the sufficient conditions — SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS — and its several Figure it Out sets apply them to determine, justify, and express congruence and to deduce equal parts, parallelism, and angle bisection from congruent triangles.\n\nSection 9.3 proves the angle properties of isosceles and equilateral triangles using congruence as the tool. Starting from an isosceles triangle with AB = AC and ∠A = 80°, it constructs the altitude from A to the base BC, meeting it at D, and shows ∆ADB ≅ ∆ADC by the RHS condition (equal sides AB and AC as hypotenuses, the common side AD, and the right angles at D), from which ∠B = ∠C follow as corresponding parts of congruent triangles. This establishes the general result that in any triangle the angles opposite equal sides are equal. Applying the same fact twice to an equilateral triangle — AB = AC gives ∠B = ∠C, and AB = BC gives ∠A = ∠C — shows all three angles are equal; since they must add up to 180°, each equals 60°. The section emphasises that these facts have been deduced purely from the notion of congruence, invites students to verify them by construction, and displays congruent triangles in real structures such as the Louvre pyramid in Paris, the Egyptian Pyramid of Giza, dome and rangoli designs, and the Howrah Bridge. Its concluding Figure it Out set asks students to read a congruence statement (∆AIR ≅ ∆FLY) for its corresponding parts, test five measurement cases for congruence with reasons, prove parallelism from congruent triangles, show that a square's diagonal splits it into triangles congruent in several different ways, and find missing angles from segments marked with equal ticks.",

  "enumerated_worked_examples": [],

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 40-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 40 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

OUTPUT — exactly this JSON object, nothing else:
{
  "synthesis_unit": {
    "activity_title": "…",
    "pedagogical_method": "one of: Discovery · Problem-solving · Play-way · Inductive ·
      Deductive — the method this unit runs on",
    "section_goal": "recall | reason | apply — the goal this unit works at",
    "teacher_notes": "a few sentences: how the sitting runs, what to watch for, and the
      chapter method each problem needs — NOT the solutions, which are in the table",
    "visual_aids": [
      {"type": "table",
        "title": "Problems and solutions",
        "table": "No. | Problem | Solution\n1 | … | …\n2 | … | …"}
    ],
    "materials": ["…"],
    "time_bands": [
      {"minutes": "0-N", "activity": "…"},
      …bands in sequence, integer boundaries, last band ends at 40…
    ],
    "textbook_items_in_class": [],
    "homework": []
  }
}
No other keys — the platform carries the unit's number, duration, section coverage and
synthesis marker itself.

  "sections": [
    { "ref": "section 10.1", "title": "A Quick Recap of Integers", "section_goal": ["recall", "apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 10.2", "title": "Multiplication of Integers", "section_goal": ["reason", "apply"] }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 10.1 recalls integer addition and subtraction and applies signed numbers to model movement and direction. It opens with Rakesh's puzzle — find two numbers given their sum (25) and difference (11) — solved by systematic guess-and-check tabulation of first number, second number, sum, and difference rather than by any formula, then extended to a negative difference (-11), where the section observes that simply swapping the pair from the first puzzle (7 and 18) gives the answer. A Figure it Out set asks for several more sum-and-difference pairs, including cases with negative sums and negative differences, and the puzzle is turned into a partner game that students can later perform as a 'magic trick'. The section then builds the carrom-coin model: a coin struck rightward by a units and then by b units lands at P = a + b, and once strikes can go in either direction, rightward is taken as positive and leftward as negative, so that a rightward strike of 5 followed by a leftward strike of 7 gives 5 + (-7) = -2, placing the coin two units to the left of zero. This models two pieces of information at once — magnitude (distance) and direction (sign) — on the number line, and students answer questions about a missing movement given the final position and about the final position after a chain of strikes 1, -2, 3, -4, …, -10, and compare magnitudes and directions from given diagrams. The section then recalls the Grade 6 token model — a green token for +1, a red token for -1, the two together forming a zero pair that cancels — and uses it to compute (+7) - (+18): since there are not enough positives to remove eighteen, eleven zero pairs are added first, then 18 positives are removed, leaving 11 negatives, or -11. This reinforces that subtracting a number is the same as adding its additive inverse, with the additive inverse of an integer a written as -a, so that 7 - 18 = 7 + (-18) and 4 - (-12) = 4 + 12.\n\nSection 10.2 reasons out the rules and properties of integer multiplication and division and applies them to expressions and real contexts. It extends the token model from addition to multiplication: 4 × 2 means placing two green tokens into an empty bag four times (giving 8), while 4 × (-2) places two red tokens four times (giving -8). When the multiplier is negative, tokens are removed instead of placed, so (-4) × 2 requires putting in four sets of two zero pairs and then removing the positives, leaving -8; and (-4) × (-2) removes negatives to leave +8. These four cases — 4×2=8, 4×(-2)=-8, (-4)×2=-8, (-4)×(-2)=8 — are then confirmed by a sequence of multiplication patterns, where for a positive multiplicand each unit decrease in the multiplier decreases the product by the multiplicand, and for a negative multiplicand it increases the product, with the pattern extended smoothly below zero and displayed in the four 'times 3' tables. From these the sign rules are stated: like signs give a positive product, unlike signs a negative product, and the magnitude is unaffected by sign. The section establishes 1 × a = a and -1 × a = -a for all integers, then argues that multiplication is commutative (a × b = b × a) by separating magnitude and sign and checking that neither changes on swapping. It introduces Brahmagupta's Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628 CE) rules, which use fortune (dhana) for positive and debt (ṛṇa) for negative quantities and give the first articulation of sign rules for both multiplication and division. Two worked examples apply this — exam marking with positive and negative marks (Example 1) and a mining-shaft elevator moving above and below ground, modelled both by subtraction and by signed speed (Example 2). The section presents a magic-grid game whose product is invariant to the numbers chosen, then converts division into a multiplication question ('what times 25 gives -100?') to derive the division sign rules a ÷ -b = -(a÷b), -a ÷ b = -(a÷b), and -a ÷ -b = a÷b. It then studies expressions: it shows integer multiplication is associative and distributive over addition using regrouping and rectangular token arrangements of green and red tokens, verifies associativity by evaluating a product such as 25 × -6 × 12 in several groupings and orders, works out the sign of a product of many integers from repeated multiplication by -1, and explores 'pattern machines' that compute a + b - c and invite students to build their own. Its extensive Figure it Out sets apply all of this to profit-and-loss, freezing temperatures, a modified integer Collatz iteration, an alien 'pibs' currency puzzle with only +13 and -9 coins, the ordering of large signed expressions, and open-ended maximum/minimum and fill-in-the-blank tasks, and the chapter closes with the traditional board game Terhüchü from Assam and Nagaland.",

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 40-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 40 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

OUTPUT — exactly this JSON object, nothing else:
{
  "synthesis_unit": {
    "activity_title": "…",
    "pedagogical_method": "one of: Discovery · Problem-solving · Play-way · Inductive ·
      Deductive — the method this unit runs on",

      chapter method each problem needs — NOT the solutions, which are in the table",

      {"type": "table",
        "title": "Problems and solutions",
        "table": "No. | Problem | Solution\n1 | … | …\n2 | … | …"}
    ],
    "materials": ["…"],
    "time_bands": [
      {"minutes": "0-N", "activity": "…"},
      …bands in sequence, integer boundaries, last band ends at 40…
    ],

  }
}

  "stage": "middle",
  "subject": "mathematics",

  "chapter_number": 11,
  "chapter_title": "Finding Common Ground",
  "sections": [
    { "ref": "section 11.1", "title": "The Greatest of All", "section_goal": ["recall", "apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 11.2", "title": "Least, but not Last!", "section_goal": ["recall", "apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 11.3", "title": "Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!", "section_goal": ["reason", "apply"] }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 11.1 recalls factors and primes and applies prime factorisation to compute the Highest Common Factor. It opens with Sameeksha tiling a 12 ft × 16 ft room with the largest possible whole-number square tile: the side must be a common factor of 12 and 16, whose common factors are 1, 2, 4, so the largest tile is 4 ft. This motivates the definition of the Highest Common Factor (HCF), also called the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD), as the greatest of the common factors, reinforced by Lekhana packing 84 kg and 108 kg of rice into equal whole-number bags and by the Grade 6 'Jump Jackpot' game, where the longest jump landing on both treasure numbers equals their HCF. Because listing all factors is cumbersome and error-prone for numbers with many factors, the section revisits primes — a number greater than 1 whose only factors are 1 and itself — and prime factorisation, establishing through examples such as 90 = 3×3×2×5 that the resulting prime factors are always the same regardless of the order in which the factorising is done, and introduces a compact division method for finding a prime factorisation (for example 105 = 3×5×7 and 30 = 2×3×5). It then shows how every factor of a number is a 'subpart' of its prime factorisation — reordering 840 = 2×2×2×3×5×7 shows 28 is a factor with co-factor 30 — and systematically lists all factors of 225 from its primes. Anshu's claim that larger numbers have longer prime factorisations is introduced as a conjecture and disproved by a counterexample (121 = 11×11). Worked Examples 1–5 find common factors and the HCF of 45 and 75, 112 and 84, 96 and 275, 30 and 72, and 225 and 750, leading to the rule: take each common prime the minimum number of times it occurs across the numbers.\n\nSection 11.2 recalls multiples and applies prime factorisation to compute the Lowest Common Multiple. It opens with Anshu and Guna making torans from 6 cm and 8 cm cloth strips: the shortest common length is a common multiple of 6 and 8, and the smallest, 24 cm, is their Lowest Common Multiple (LCM), the least of the common multiples. A sweet-shop gajak problem (free every 7 days for the shop's Monday cycle, visited every 10 days) gives the LCM of 7 and 10 as 70 days, and the Grade 6 'Idli-Vada' game reinforces that the first common call-out is the LCM. Since listing multiples is tedious for larger numbers, the section develops the prime-factorisation method: comparing a number with its multiple shows the multiple's factorisation contains the number's, so a common multiple must contain each number's prime subpart. Worked Example 6 (14 and 35 → 70) and Example 7 (96 and 360 → 1440) build the LCM by taking each prime the maximum number of times it occurs in either factorisation, and the method extends to more than two numbers.\n\nSection 11.3 reasons about patterns and properties relating HCF and LCM and applies an efficient combined procedure. It observes that when one number is a factor of the other, the HCF is the smaller number, and formalises this as a general statement, introducing the terms 'general statement' and 'generalisation' and describing such pairs with algebra (n and 5n, with HCF = n). Figure it Out sets ask students to make and explain general statements about the HCF and LCM of consecutive even, consecutive odd, even, consecutive, co-prime numbers, and multiples of 3. The section explores what happens to the HCF when both numbers are doubled (it doubles, since each gains a factor of 2), and when both numbers are multiples of a common number. It also examines pairs where both numbers are multiples of the same number (such as 14×6 and 14×9, whose HCF is 42) and asks when the HCF equals the common multiplier. It presents an efficient division procedure that divides both numbers by common primes simultaneously until the quotients share no common factor, reads off the HCF from the column of divisors and the LCM from the divisors together with the final quotients, and shows Guna's and Anshu's shortcuts of dividing by larger common factors (such as 50, or 10 then 7) all at once, noting one need not divide by a single prime at a time. It then establishes the key property HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers by examining how common and non-common prime factors distribute between the HCF and the LCM, and asks whether it extends to three numbers. Its extensive Figure it Out set applies all of this to repeating colour patterns, factor-and-multiple checks, HCF/LCM stated as prime factorisations, a cowherd folklore problem from Karnataka, cube-packing, divisibility puzzles including 'Fire in the Mountain' and a dog-and-rabbit chase, and a fraction-sum problem posed by the Indian mathematician Mahaviracharya (850 CE).",
  "enumerated_activities": [],
  "enumerated_worked_examples": [
    { "id": "WE-1", "source_section": "section 11.1", "book_ref": "Example 1, section 11.1 p.52", "description": "Find the common factors and HCF of 45 and 75. Using 45 = 3×3×5 and 75 = 3×5×5, the common subparts are 3, 5, 15, so common factors are 1, 3, 5, 15 and HCF = 15." },
    { "id": "WE-2", "source_section": "section 11.1", "book_ref": "Example 2, section 11.1 p.52", "description": "Find the common factors and HCF of 112 and 84. Using 112 = 2×2×2×2×7 and 84 = 2×2×3×7, the largest common subpart is 2×2×7 = 28, so HCF = 28." },
    { "id": "WE-3", "source_section": "section 11.1", "book_ref": "Example 3, section 11.1 p.53", "description": "Find the common factors and HCF of 96 and 275. Since 96 = 2×2×2×2×2×3 and 275 = 5×5×11 share no prime subpart, the only common factor is 1, which is also the HCF." },
    { "id": "WE-4", "source_section": "section 11.1", "book_ref": "Example 4, section 11.1 p.53", "description": "Find the HCF of 30 and 72 directly. From 30 = 2×3×5 and 72 = 2×2×2×3×3, take each common prime the minimum number of times (one 2, one 3): HCF = 2×3 = 6." },
    { "id": "WE-5", "source_section": "section 11.1", "book_ref": "Example 5, section 11.1 p.53", "description": "Find the HCF of 225 and 750. From 225 = 3×3×5×5 and 750 = 2×3×5×5×5, take one 3 and two 5s: HCF = 3×5×5 = 75." },
    { "id": "WE-6", "source_section": "section 11.2", "book_ref": "Example 6, section 11.2 p.56–57", "description": "Find the LCM of 14 and 35. From 14 = 2×7 and 35 = 5×7, the LCM must contain 2×7 and 5×7 as subparts: the lowest is 2×5×7 = 70." },
    { "id": "WE-7", "source_section": "section 11.2", "book_ref": "Example 7, section 11.2 p.57", "description": "Find the LCM of 96 and 360. From 96 = 2×2×2×2×2×3 and 360 = 2×2×2×3×3×5, take the maximum occurrences of each prime (five 2s, two 3s, one 5): LCM = 1440." }

system.text:
ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 40-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 40 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

OUTPUT — exactly this JSON object, nothing else:
{
  "synthesis_unit": {
    "activity_title": "…",
    "pedagogical_method": "one of: Discovery · Problem-solving · Play-way · Inductive ·
      Deductive — the method this unit runs on",
    "section_goal": "recall | reason | apply — the goal this unit works at",
    "teacher_notes": "a few sentences: how the sitting runs, what to watch for, and the
      chapter method each problem needs — NOT the solutions, which are in the table",
    "visual_aids": [
      {"type": "table",
        "title": "Problems and solutions",
        "table": "No. | Problem | Solution\n1 | … | …\n2 | … | …"}
    ],
    "materials": ["…"],
    "time_bands": [
      {"minutes": "0-N", "activity": "…"},
      …bands in sequence, integer boundaries, last band ends at 40…
    ],
    "textbook_items_in_class": [],

  }
}
No other keys — the platform carries the unit's number, duration, section coverage and
synthesis marker itself.
