  "prose_summary": "Section 12.1 recalls the decimal place-value system and applies it to convert between fractions and decimals. It reviews that decimals extend the Indian place-value system to tenths, hundredths, thousandths and their sums, reading 27.53 as 2 tens, 7 units, 5 tenths, 3 hundredths. A fraction–decimal game between Jonali and Pallabi and a spice-buying context (50 g, 100 g, 25 g, 250 g expressed in kilograms) lead students to write fractions with denominators 10, 100, 1000 as sums of tenths, hundredths, and thousandths and as decimals. The section notes that multiplying and dividing decimals will be shown to be natural extensions of the procedures already learnt for counting numbers and for fractions. From a pattern in these problems the section derives the rule for dividing a number by a power of ten — write the number with a decimal point at the end, count the zeroes in the divisor, and move the point left by that many places, inserting leading zeroes if needed — illustrated by 123 ÷ 10 = 12.3, 24 ÷ 100 = 0.24, 12 ÷ 1000 = 0.012, and 12345 ÷ 1000 = 12.345.\n\nSection 12.2 applies fraction multiplication to multiply decimals and then reasons out a general placement rule. Worked Examples 1–5 — five pens at ₹9.5, a car covering 12.5 km per litre for 7.5 litres, Ajay's twice-daily walk of 0.827 km for six days, the area of a 5.7 cm × 13.3 cm rectangle, and 5.8 × 1.24 — each convert the decimals to fractions over powers of ten, multiply numerators and denominators, and read off the decimal product. Tabulating the number of digits after the decimal point in the multiplier, multiplicand, and product, the section frames the rule: multiply the numbers with the decimal points removed, then place the point so that the number of decimal places equals the sum of the decimal places in the two factors (so 596 × 248 = 147808 gives 5.96 × 24.8 = 147.808). It then examines when a product is greater or less than the numbers multiplied, tabulating three situations — both numbers greater than 1, both between 0 and 1, and one of each — mirroring the behaviour of fractions. Its Figure it Out set applies decimal multiplication to cloth, stationery, coin-stack height, orange prices, wholesale profit, and sign-of-size reasoning about which products are less than 1.\n\nSection 12.3 applies several division procedures and reasons about terminating and non-terminating quotients. It divides decimals by powers of ten by moving the point left (3.9 ÷ 10 = 0.39, 3.9 ÷ 100 = 0.039), then converts fractions to equivalent fractions with denominators 10, 100, 1000 (29 ÷ 2 = 14.5, 29 ÷ 4 = 7.25). Where no such equivalent fraction exists, it develops division using place value — 'long division' — regrouping thousands into hundreds, ones into tenths, tenths into hundredths, and so on, worked through 1324 ÷ 4 = 331, 1325 ÷ 4 = 331.25, 237 ÷ 8 = 29.625, a decimal dividend 9.5 ÷ 4 = 2.375, and 0.06 ÷ 5 = 0.012, always placing the decimal point in the quotient when ones are first regrouped into tenths. For a decimal divisor it multiplies dividend and divisor by the same power of ten to make the divisor a whole number (126 ÷ 2.5 = 50.4; 4.68 ÷ 0.13 = 468 ÷ 13). It then investigates 10 ÷ 3 = 3.333…, which never ends because the remainder is always 1, and 1 ÷ 7 = 0.142857…, whose remainders and quotient digits repeat in a cycle, leading to the 'magic number' 142857 and Emil Artin's still-unsolved 1927 conjecture about cyclic numbers, before relating the dividend, divisor, and quotient when the divisor is a decimal.\n\nSection 12.4 applies decimal multiplication to the leap-year problem and reasons through successive calendar corrections. Since the Earth takes 365.2422 days to orbit the Sun, 0.2422 × 100 = 24.22 extra days accumulate over a century, motivating the leap-year rule of adding a day every fourth year. Using divisibility decision charts (divisible by 4? by 100? by 400?), the section builds expressions for the number of calendar days over 100 and 1000 years — for example (24 × 366) + (76 × 365) = 36,524 days for a century once the 100th year is excluded, and a four-term sum for a millennium once the 400th year is restored — and compares them with the actual 100 × 365.2422 = 36,524.22 and 1000 × 365.2422 = 3,65,242.2 days, showing how the every-4, skip-100, keep-400 scheme progressively narrows the gap. It also observes, through a table of 1/2, 1/(2×2), … and 1/5, 1/(5×5), …, that fractions whose denominators are built only from 2s and 5s give terminating decimals. Its Figure it Out set applies decimal arithmetic to unit-price comparison, number-line reading, profit, shelf-packing, unit conversions, a Patiganita problem of Sridharacharya, fill-in-the-boxes products, and quotient patterns.",

system.text:
ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 40-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 40 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

OUTPUT — exactly this JSON object, nothing else:
{
  "synthesis_unit": {
    "activity_title": "…",
    "pedagogical_method": "one of: Discovery · Problem-solving · Play-way · Inductive ·
      Deductive — the method this unit runs on",

    "teacher_notes": "a few sentences: how the sitting runs, what to watch for, and the
      chapter method each problem needs — NOT the solutions, which are in the table",
    "visual_aids": [
      {"type": "table",
        "title": "Problems and solutions",
        "table": "No. | Problem | Solution\n1 | … | …\n2 | … | …"}
    ],
    "materials": ["…"],
    "time_bands": [
      {"minutes": "0-N", "activity": "…"},
      …bands in sequence, integer boundaries, last band ends at 40…
    ],

  }
}

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

{
  "stage": "middle",
  "subject": "mathematics",
  "grade": "vii",
  "chapter_number": 13,
  "chapter_title": "Connecting the Dots",
  "sections": [
    { "ref": "section 13.1", "title": "Of Questions and Statements", "section_goal": ["recall", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 13.2", "title": "Representative Values", "section_goal": ["apply", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 13.3", "title": "Visualising Data", "section_goal": ["apply", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 13.4", "title": "Data Detective", "section_goal": ["reason", "apply"] }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 13.1 defines the basic ideas of statistical thinking and reasons about what makes a question statistical. Beginning with guessing gender from height, it introduces the statistical statement — a claim or summary about a phenomenon expressed in numerical values, proportions, probabilities, or predictions — through everyday examples about batting consistency, cycling time, and village population. It then defines a statistical question as one that can be answered by collecting and analysing data (such as 'How tall are Grade 7 students in our school?' or 'Are onions typically costlier in Yahapur or Wahapur?'), noting that such questions expect variation in the answers and so require data to be gathered, analysed, and turned into conclusions. Students are asked to classify a list of everyday questions as statistical or not, before the section names statistics as the study of collecting, organising, analysing, interpreting, and presenting data, and sets up the chapter's aim of using data and graphs to answer such questions.\n\nSection 13.2 applies the ideas of representative value and reasons about which measure best summarises data. Using cricket scores of two players across series of different lengths, it weighs several proposed comparisons (highest single score, total runs, consistency) and shows the total can mislead when the two players played different numbers of matches, and introduces the arithmetic mean (average) as the sum of values divided by their number, understood also as fair-share — worked through guava-sharing groups and daily hibiscus blooms — and notes ancient Indian terms for the mean (samamiti, samarajju by Brahmagupta, samīkaraṇa by Mahāvīrācārya, sāmya by Śrīpati). It then examines the onion-price data of Yahapur and Wahapur, describing data by its minimum, maximum, total, range, and average and visualising it with a dot plot that sorts values and reveals clustering and spread. Through family-height, short-story, and newspaper-page examples it introduces the median (the middle value of sorted data, or the average of the two middle values), the outlier (a value that deviates greatly from the rest), and shows how an outlier pulls the mean away from the median, so that a low outlier gives mean < median and a high outlier gives mean > median. Naming mean and median as measures of central tendency — the tendency of values to pile up around a central value — it also stresses variability, the extremes (minimum and maximum) of the data. It works through the heights of a whole class split into boys and girls, a minute-estimation activity comparing two groups, a 'zero median but high total' cricket example, and zero-versus-no-value cases (a player scoring 0 versus not playing, and a mango tree's off-season months) where only the relevant values should be counted, and closes with a historical note on how a 16-foot 'rod' in 1500s Europe was effectively the arithmetic mean of sixteen men's feet.\n\nSection 13.3 applies graphical representations and reasons about what they show. It combines the two single-column onion-price graphs into one clustered (double) column graph with bars side by side and a stated scale, then presents a two-step process for reading graphs — identify what is given (organisation, scale, patterns) and infer from what is given (analyse and interpret) — applied to worldwide rocket-launch data by organisation and year and to monthly daylight-hour data for Helsinki and Wellington, drawing out that their inverted seasonal patterns reflect opposite hemispheres. It also notes design choices — using colour and pattern fills for greyscale readability, and keeping a time order for months but not for unordered categories such as organisations. A cricket runs-per-over double bar graph with wicket markers is read to answer questions about who batted first, over-by-over scores, and the target. Its Figure it Out set has students read an animal-speed infographic and construct double-bar graphs for superpower preferences across two grades, two days of Jodhpur temperatures, and electric-vehicle registrations across several states and years.\n\nSection 13.4 reasons about the stories and mysteries data can reveal and applies analysis to rich real datasets. Comparing boy and girl heights across grades and schools, and a survey table of average heights of Indian boys and girls aged 5 to 19 across 1989–2019, it asks which statements can be justified from the data, between which successive ages boys and girls grow the most, and how to extrapolate the trend to 2029 — training students to separate claims the data supports from those it does not, and cautioning that one or two schools' data cannot be generalised to a whole country. Its extensive Figure it Out set includes dot-plot comparisons, a scoring table with a did-not-play entry, quiz-score comparison, several double-bar-graph constructions, grouping students by a threshold height, mean-height inference across sections, and a series of individual, long-term, and small-group data-collection projects (sentence and name lengths, an 'In and Out' tracker, family heights, and time estimation), closing with a number-lock deduction puzzle.",
  "enumerated_activities": [],
  "enumerated_worked_examples": [],

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 40-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 40 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

{
  "stage": "middle",
  "subject": "mathematics",
  "grade": "vii",
  "chapter_number": 14,
  "chapter_title": "Constructions and Tilings",
  "sections": [
    { "ref": "section 14.1", "title": "Geometric Constructions", "section_goal": ["apply", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 14.2", "title": "Tiling", "section_goal": ["apply", "reason"] }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 14.1 constructs a family of geometric figures with a ruler and compass and justifies each construction through congruence. Starting from the Grade 6 'Eyes' design, it shows that the two arc-centres lie at equal distances from the endpoints X and Y of a supporting segment, defines bisection and the perpendicular bisector, and constructs the perpendicular bisector by drawing equal-radius arcs above and below XY and joining their intersections. It justifies this rigorously: showing ∆ABX ≅ ∆ABY (SSS) and then ∆AOX ≅ ∆AOY (SAS) proves O is the midpoint and AB is perpendicular to XY, and it establishes the general fact that any point equidistant from X and Y lies on the perpendicular bisector. It also shows how eyes of different shapes arise by choosing different pairs of points on that bisector as arc-centres, and stresses that this compass method of finding a midpoint is more accurate than measuring with a scale. Figure it Out tasks probe whether equal radii and both-side arcs are really necessary. The method is extended to construct a 90° angle at a point on a line by treating that point as the midpoint of a segment and drawing the perpendicular bisector through it, needing only one pair of arcs since the point is already known to lie on the bisector. A historical passage describes how the Vedic Śulba-Sūtras — geometric texts of the Vedic period used to lay out fire altars, and part of the Vedāṅgas — construct the same perpendicular bisector with a stretched rope (Kātyāyana-Śulbasūtra 1.2), using pegs at X and Y and the rope's midpoint pulled taut above and below. The section then develops angle bisection — drawing congruent triangles ∆OBC ≅ ∆OAC (SSS) so that OC bisects ∠AOB — giving a 45° angle by bisecting a right angle, and a general method to copy an angle by transferring an isosceles triangle's base (∆ABC ≅ ∆XYZ by SSS). This 45° angle is exactly what the eight-fold petal design needs, since 360° divided into eight equal parts gives 45°. Copying an angle underlies the construction of a line parallel to a given line: a transversal is drawn, and the corresponding angle at a chosen point is copied so that the new line makes equal corresponding angles with the transversal and is therefore parallel. The section also constructs decorative arches — a trefoil arch from equal angles and equal arms at two points, and a pointed arch from two equal segments and their midpoints. Using a 60° angle built from an equilateral triangle (two equal-radius arcs from the ends of a segment), the section constructs a regular hexagon, first reasoning that six congruent equilateral triangles can meet at a single centre precisely because their 60° angles sum to 360° and so cover the region around the point without gaps or overlaps, giving a hexagon with equal sides and 120° angles. From these it derives 30° and 15° angles by further bisection, a 120° angle, and a 6-pointed star whose six points are equilateral triangles. Its many Figure it Out sets ask students to construct angles and their bisectors, parallel-line pairs, an 8-petalled figure, trefoil and pointed arches, an inflexed arc, an optical-illusion figure, and a perpendicular to a line through an external point.\n\nSection 14.2 explores tiling — covering a region without gaps or overlaps — and reasons about when it is possible. It opens with the Chinese tangram, whose seven pieces (from a divided square) are rearranged into figures, then asks whether rectangular grids can be tiled by 2 × 1 tiles. It shows a 4 × 6 grid can be tiled, and reasons that a 5 × 7 grid (35 unit squares) cannot, since each tile covers exactly two squares and 35 is odd. It develops general strategies for m × n grids by the parities of m and n — a grid with an even number of rows can be tiled column by column — and examines grids with a unit square removed, asking when the remaining even-count region is tileable. It then introduces a powerful black-and-white colouring argument: colouring the grid like a chessboard, each 2 × 1 tile must cover exactly one black and one white square, so any tileable region must have equal numbers of black and white squares; the region in Fig. 6.14, with 8 white and 6 black squares, therefore can never be tiled — a striking case where deliberately making the problem more complicated by adding colour actually makes it easier to settle. It then turns to tiling the entire plane, showing squares, equilateral triangles, and regular hexagons all work, noting tilings with multiple and non-regular shapes including M. C. Escher's animal tilings and a tiling discovered only in 2023, and observing the hexagonal cells of bee hives and wasp nests as natural tilings. Its Figure it Out sets ask whether particular region-and-tile combinations can be tiled.",

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 40-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 40 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

{
  "stage": "middle",
  "subject": "mathematics",
  "grade": "vii",
  "chapter_number": 15,
  "chapter_title": "Finding the Unknown",
  "sections": [
    { "ref": "section 15.1", "title": "Find the Unknowns", "section_goal": ["apply", "recall"] },
    { "ref": "section 15.2", "title": "Solving Equations Systematically", "section_goal": ["apply", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 15.3", "title": "Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake", "section_goal": ["reason", "apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 15.4", "title": "A Pinch of History", "section_goal": ["recall", "apply"] }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 15.1 applies balance reasoning to find unknowns and then introduces the language of equations. It opens with a series of weighing-scale pictures whose two plates balance, asking students to find unknown weights, and gives the key idea through a hint: removing equal weights from both plates keeps the scale balanced. It then turns to a matchstick sequence whose position n uses 2n + 1 sticks, so finding which arrangement uses 99 sticks means solving 2n + 1 = 99. This motivates the definition of an equation as a statement of equality between two algebraic expressions written with an equal sign between them, with the Left Hand Side (LHS) and Right Hand Side (RHS), and solving meaning finding the letter-number value for which the LHS equals the RHS. Several examples of equations (3x + 4 = 7, 20 = y − 3, a/3 = 50, 2z + 4 = 5z − 14) are given. Students revisit the balance pictures — denoting an unknown weight by a letter — to frame equations such as 2e = 6 and 4 + 2y = 16, solve them, check the solutions against the weights they found earlier, and are asked to frame and solve five equations of their own.\n\nSection 15.2 applies systematic methods to solve equations and reasons about why they work. It first shows the trial-and-error method (substituting values until LHS = RHS), works it through for 2n + 1 = 99 to reach n = 49, and notes its inefficiency, then establishes that performing the same operation on both sides of an equation preserves equality — the algebraic version of the balance property. Through arithmetic Examples 1–4 it uses inverse operations (subtracting a term, dividing by a factor, adding an additive inverse, dividing by a fractional factor) to isolate an expression, then solves 5x − 4 = 7, 11y + (−5) = 61, and 6y + 7 = 4y + 21, checking solutions by substitution and bringing unknown terms to one side. It distils the shortcut rules of transposition — a term added or subtracted on one side, when removed, appears as its additive inverse on the other side (so 2y + 7 = 21 becomes 2y = 21 − 7); a factor removed from a product means the other side is divided by it (2y = 14 becomes y = 14 ÷ 2); and a divisor removed means the other side is multiplied by it (u/15 = 6 becomes u = 6 × 15). It then forms and solves equations for real problems: Ranjana's square-tile pattern (3k + 1 = 100), Madhubanti's party budget (solved several ways by different children), Jahnavi and Sunita's equal savings after 7 months, 28(x + 4) + 300 = 1000 solved by several routes, Riyaz's think-of-a-number trick, and Ramesh and Suresh's marbles (reducing two unknowns to one). A 'Generating Equations' part reverses the process, asking students to write equations with a given solution and to build chains of equivalent equations by performing the same operation on both sides, and Example 13 asks for a real-life situation modelling 100x + 75 = 250. Its Figure it Out sets solve varied equations, frame equations with a given solution or no solution, and pose digit, brick, and fraction puzzles.\n\nSection 15.3 reasons critically about worked solutions. It presents nine equations, each already solved with the steps shown, and asks students to decide whether each step is correct, describe any mistake (such as moving a term without changing its sign or dropping a coefficient), correct it, and solve the equation properly — turning the balance and transposition rules into a tool for critical error analysis rather than mere procedure-following.\n\nSection 15.4 recalls the history of algebra and applies an ancient formula. It explains that forming and solving equations was called bījagaṇita (bīja meaning seed) in ancient India, traces Brahmagupta's Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628 CE) as one of the earliest works of algebra, the transmission of Indian ideas to Al-Khwarizmi (c. 825 CE, whose al-jabr gives us the word algebra), and the ancient Indian notation using symbols such as yā, kā, and rū for unknowns and knowns. It notes David Mumford's remark that 'Brahmagupta is the key person in the creation of algebra as we know it'. Bhāskarāchārya's horse-and-debt problem (Example 16) is modelled and solved, and Brahmagupta's general formula x = (D − B)/(A − C) for equations of the form Ax + B = Cx + D — a method first proposed by Aryabhata and outlined by Brahmagupta — is stated and applied, and the section closes by noting that algebra lets us generalise patterns and justify claims. Its extensive Figure it Out set covers fill-in-the-blank equations, wage, taxi-fare, restaurant, angle, and grill problems, the Bakhśhāli Manuscript (300 CE) distribution problem, stick-pattern sequences, a solve-your-path maze, and a heads-and-feet puzzle about children and donkeys.",

  "enumerated_worked_examples": [
    { "id": "WE-1", "source_section": "section 15.2", "book_ref": "Example 1, section 15.2 p.169", "description": "Given 14593 − 1459 + 145 − 14 + 88 = 13353, find 14593 − 1459 + 145 − 14 by subtracting 88 from both sides (addition and subtraction as inverse operations): the value is 13265." },

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 45-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 45 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

  "chapter_number": 1,
  "chapter_title": "A Square and A Cube",
  "sections": [
    { "ref": "section 1.intro", "title": "Opening Puzzle: The Locker Problem", "section_goal": ["reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 1.1", "title": "Square Numbers", "section_goal": ["recall", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 1.1a", "title": "Patterns and Properties of Perfect Squares", "section_goal": ["reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 1.1b", "title": "Perfect Squares and Odd Numbers", "section_goal": ["reason", "apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 1.1c", "title": "Perfect Squares and Triangular Numbers", "section_goal": ["reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 1.1d", "title": "Square Roots", "section_goal": ["apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 1.2", "title": "Cubic Numbers", "section_goal": ["recall", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 1.2a", "title": "Perfect Cubes and Consecutive Odd Numbers", "section_goal": ["reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 1.2b", "title": "Cube Roots", "section_goal": ["apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 1.2c", "title": "Successive Differences", "section_goal": ["reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 1.3", "title": "A Pinch of History", "section_goal": ["recall"] }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "The chapter opens with a richly contextualised puzzle — the Queen Ratnamanjuri locker problem — in which 100 people toggle lockers in sequence and students must reason about which lockers end up open. The chapter uses this narrative hook to introduce the central concepts of square numbers and cube numbers, establishing from the outset that understanding the number of factors a number possesses is the key to identifying perfect squares.\n\nSection 1.1 defines square numbers by connecting the geometric idea of a square figure's area to the arithmetic operation of multiplying a number by itself. The section recalls that numbers expressible as n × n = n² are called square numbers or perfect squares, and extends the definition to include fractions and decimals such as (3/5)² and (2.5)².\n\nSection 1.1a reasons about and identifies the patterns and properties of perfect squares through exploration of a table of the first 30 natural numbers and their squares. Students observe which units digits are possible for perfect squares (0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 9), that squares can only end with an even number of zeros, and that the parity of a number is preserved in its square. The section invites conjectures and then justifies them, developing students' capacity to reason from patterns.\n\nSection 1.1b explains and then proves the relationship between perfect squares and consecutive odd numbers. It establishes that the sum of the first n odd numbers equals n², using both a visual proof (the inverted-L dot diagram recalled from Grade 6) and an algebraic argument (the nth odd number is 2n − 1). The section then applies this result: students can determine whether a number is a perfect square by successively subtracting odd numbers starting from 1, and can compute (n+1)² from n² by adding the next odd number.\n\nSection 1.1c reasons about the relationship between triangular numbers and square numbers. It identifies that the sum of two consecutive triangular numbers is always a perfect square, illustrated through dot-array diagrams and the pattern 1 + 3 = 4 = 2², 3 + 6 = 9 = 3², 6 + 10 = 16 = 4².\n\nSection 1.1d applies multiple methods to find square roots and determine whether a number is a perfect square. It defines square root as the inverse of squaring, introduces the √ notation, and then presents three methods: listing consecutive squares, successive subtraction of odd numbers, and prime factorisation. It further applies estimation strategies — bounding between known squares and narrowing by examining units digits — to find approximate square roots of non-perfect squares such as 250.\n\nSection 1.2 defines cubic numbers by extending the geometric idea of a cube's volume (n × n × n = n³) and identifies perfect cubes as numbers expressible as n³ for natural number n. The section recalls the sequence 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, … and then reasons about which units digits are possible for cubes, comparing with the squares case. It also introduces the culturally rich Taxicab number story of Ramanujan and Hardy (1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³), grounding number theory in mathematical history.\n\nSection 1.2a reasons about the pattern linking perfect cubes and consecutive odd numbers: 1 = 1³, 3 + 5 = 2³, 7 + 9 + 11 = 3³, and so on, where the nth cube equals the sum of n consecutive odd numbers beginning where the previous cube's group ended. Students apply this to determine the sum of a given group of consecutive odd numbers (91 to 109 = 10³ = 1000).\n\nSection 1.2b applies prime factorisation to determine cube roots. It establishes that a number is a perfect cube if and only if each prime factor appears in multiples of three in its prime factorisation, and the cube root is found by taking one factor from each triplet. The section works through examples (3375 = 3³ × 5³, so ∛3375 = 15; 500 is not a perfect cube).\n\nSection 1.2c reasons about successive differences of perfect cubes, inviting students to extend the successive-differences approach (used earlier for squares) to cubes. While squares yield constant differences at level 2 (all 2s), cubes require three levels before differences stabilise.\n\nSection 1.3 recalls the historical and etymological origins of the terms square, cube, and root, tracing the Sanskrit terms varga (square), ghana (cube), and mula (root) through Indian mathematical texts from the first century BCE to Aryabhata (499 CE) and Brahmagupta (628 CE), and showing how these concepts passed into Arabic (jidhr) and Latin (radix). This section grounds the chapter's mathematical content in the rich history of Indian mathematics.",

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 45-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 45 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

OUTPUT — exactly this JSON object, nothing else:
{
  "synthesis_unit": {
    "activity_title": "…",
    "pedagogical_method": "one of: Discovery · Problem-solving · Play-way · Inductive ·
      Deductive — the method this unit runs on",
    "section_goal": "recall | reason | apply — the goal this unit works at",
    "teacher_notes": "a few sentences: how the sitting runs, what to watch for, and the
      chapter method each problem needs — NOT the solutions, which are in the table",
    "visual_aids": [
      {"type": "table",
        "title": "Problems and solutions",
        "table": "No. | Problem | Solution\n1 | … | …\n2 | … | …"}
    ],
    "materials": ["…"],
    "time_bands": [
      {"minutes": "0-N", "activity": "…"},
      …bands in sequence, integer boundaries, last band ends at 45…
    ],
    "textbook_items_in_class": [],
    "homework": []
  }
}
No other keys — the platform carries the unit's number, duration, section coverage and
synthesis marker itself.

  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 45 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

    { "ref": "section 3.2.I", "title": "Use of Body Parts", "section_goal": ["recall"] },
    { "ref": "section 3.2.II", "title": "Tally Marks on Bones and Other Surfaces", "section_goal": ["recall"] },
    { "ref": "section 3.2.III", "title": "Number Names Obtained by Counting in Twos", "section_goal": ["recall", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 3.2.IV", "title": "The Roman Numerals", "section_goal": ["apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 3.3.I", "title": "The Egyptian Number System", "section_goal": ["apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 3.3.II", "title": "Variations on the Egyptian System and the Notion of Base", "section_goal": ["reason", "apply"] },
    { "ref": "section 3.3.III", "title": "Shortcomings of the Egyptian System", "section_goal": ["reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 3.4.I", "title": "The Mesopotamian Number System", "section_goal": ["recall", "reason"] },
    { "ref": "section 3.4.II", "title": "The Mayan Number System", "section_goal": ["recall"] },
    { "ref": "section 3.4.III", "title": "The Chinese Number System", "section_goal": ["recall"] },
    { "ref": "section 3.4.IV", "title": "The Hindu Number System", "section_goal": ["reason"] }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 3.1 identifies the historical context for the chapter by tracing the origins of counting to the Stone Age: humans needed to track food, animals, trade goods, and celestial events. It introduces the origin of the modern number system in ancient India, noting that the Yajurveda Samhita named numbers as powers of ten, that the Bakhshali manuscript (c. 3rd century CE) contains the earliest known use of ten digits including zero, and that Aryabhata (499 CE) systematised the Indian system. The chapter then traces the transmission of Hindu numerals through the Arab world (Al-Khwarizmi, Al-Kindi, c. 825–830 CE) to Europe via Fibonacci (c. 1200 CE), ultimately displacing Roman numerals by the 17th century.\n\nSection 3.2.I recalls the use of body parts as counting tools, illustrated by a group from Papua New Guinea who use 27 body-part locations as a standard counting sequence, showing that physical objects can serve as a number system.\n\nSection 3.2.II recalls tally marks on bones as one of the oldest known forms of number representation, describing the Lebombo bone (~44,000 years old, 29 notches) and the Ishango bone (20,000–35,000 years old) as archaeological evidence that notch-counting was a widespread early practice.\n\nSection 3.2.III identifies and then reasons about the Gumulgal (Australia), Bakairi (South America), and Bushmen (South Africa) number systems, all of which count in twos using compound names (e.g., ukasar-ukasar-urapon for 5). The section reasons that counting in groups — here groups of two — is more efficient than a pure tally, and introduces the general idea that a group size (2, 5, 10, or 20) can serve as the organising unit of a number system. It connects this to the human perceptual limit of immediately recognising collections of fewer than five objects.\n\nSection 3.2.IV applies Roman numeral conventions by introducing landmark numbers (I, V, X, L, C, D, M) and demonstrating how any number is grouped into these landmarks from largest to smallest. The section shows that grouping by a sequence of different landmark numbers (rather than a single group size) is more efficient for large-number representation, but identifies that Roman arithmetic — particularly multiplication and division — is cumbersome because the landmark numbers are not powers of a fixed base.\n\nSection 3.3.I applies the Egyptian number system, in which landmark numbers are successive powers of 10 (1, 10, 100, … 10^7) each assigned a unique hieroglyphic symbol. Numbers are represented by grouping into these landmark numbers and concatenating the symbols. The section demonstrates encoding (e.g., 324 = 100+100+100+10+10+4) and connects the Egyptian approach to the idea of a base.\n\nSection 3.3.II reasons through and then applies the generalisation of the Egyptian idea: any fixed integer n ≥ 2 can serve as a base, with landmark numbers being the powers of n. The section constructs a base-5 system with its own symbols, represents numbers in it (e.g., 143 = 125+5+5+5+1+1+1), and formalises the definition of a base-n number system. It then applies these systems to carry out addition and multiplication in both Egyptian and base-5 notations, showing that the base structure makes arithmetic systematic: multiplying any landmark number by the base yields the next landmark number, and the distributive law operates cleanly across landmark-number decompositions. The decimal abacus (11th century, lines representing powers of 10, counters on lines) is described as a calculation device that leveraged the base-10 structure.\n\nSection 3.3.III reasons about the fundamental shortcoming of the Egyptian system: as numbers grow arbitrarily large, new symbols are needed for each new power of ten, so the system cannot represent all numbers with a finite symbol set. This sets up the need for a positional (place value) system.\n\nSection 3.4.I introduces the Mesopotamian sexagesimal (base-60) system and then reasons through the key innovation of place value. Numbers 1–59 are represented using two symbols (for 1 and for 10), and each position in a numeral corresponds to a successive power of 60. Dropping the landmark-number labels and relying on position alone allows any number to be written with a finite symbol set. The section defines a positional number system (place value system) and notes the residual defect: blank spaces to represent skipped powers of 60 created ambiguity. The later Mesopotamian solution — a placeholder symbol (analogous to 0) used in medial positions — is introduced but its limitation (not used at the end of numerals) is also noted.\n\nSection 3.4.II recalls the Mayan civilisation's independently developed place value system (3rd–10th centuries CE), which used a dot for 1, a bar for 5, and a seashell symbol as a zero placeholder. The Mayan system is almost base-20 but with landmark numbers 1, 20, 360, 7200 (not 400 = 20²) due to calendar influences. Despite lacking a true base structure, its place value notation and zero placeholder are recognised as important advances.\n\nSection 3.4.III recalls the Chinese rod numeral system (decimal, base-10), in which Zong (vertical) and Heng (horizontal) rod symbols alternate by position to distinguish adjacent place values. Like Mesopotamian notation, blank spaces indicated absent powers; the more uniform symbol sizes made blank spaces easier to identify. The Chinese system with a zero symbol would constitute a fully developed place value system.\n\nSection 3.4.IV reasons about why the Hindu number system is the culmination of all the ideas surveyed. It is a base-10 place value system with 10 distinct digit symbols (0–9), where 0 functions not merely as a placeholder but as a number in its own right on which arithmetic operations are defined. Aryabhata used 0 in computations (499 CE); Brahmagupta codified arithmetic properties of 0 and negative numbers (628 CE), creating what modern algebra calls a ring. The section closes with a summary diagram of the five evolutionary ideas: counting in groups, using landmark numbers, choosing powers of a base, using position for landmark numbers, and zero as digit and number.",

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 45-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 45 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 4.1 defines rectangles and squares and then reasons out their diagonal and angle properties through a sequence of ten deductions driven by congruence arguments. The section opens with the Carpenter's Problem: two equal wooden strips joined at their midpoints must span the vertices of a rectangle, motivating the question of what diagonal conditions force a quadrilateral to be a rectangle. Deduction 1 proves that the diagonals of a rectangle are equal using SAS congruence on triangles formed by a diagonal; Deduction 2 proves that they bisect each other using AAS congruence, so the carpenter must join the strips at their midpoints. Deduction 3 then works in reverse — starting from two equal, mutually bisecting diagonals at an arbitrary angle x, it computes all interior angles of the resulting quadrilateral algebraically and shows they are all 90°, establishing that any such diagonal configuration yields a rectangle regardless of the crossing angle. Deduction 4 further simplifies the definition: a quadrilateral in which all angles are 90° must have opposite sides equal (by AAS congruence on the two triangles formed by a diagonal), so 'all angles 90°' alone suffices as the defining condition. The section then introduces squares as the special subclass of rectangles in which all sides are equal, uses a Venn diagram to display the squares-within-rectangles containment, and poses the Carpenter's Problem for squares. Deduction 5 shows that if equal bisecting diagonals produce a square, they must cross at 90° (by SSS congruence, the two half-diagonal triangles are congruent and their shared angle must be a straight angle split equally). The section closes by listing five properties of rectangles (all angles 90°; opposite sides equal; opposite sides parallel; diagonals equal and bisecting) and five properties of squares (all sides equal; opposite sides parallel; all angles 90°; diagonals equal, bisecting, and perpendicular; diagonals bisect the corner angles).\n\nSection 4.2 reasons about a general angle-sum property of quadrilaterals. The section asks whether a quadrilateral with three right angles can have a fourth angle that is not 90°, then justifies that this is impossible by proving the angle-sum theorem. Drawing one diagonal of any quadrilateral splits it into two triangles, each with angle sum 180°; the six triangle angles pair up exactly into the four quadrilateral angles, giving a total of 360°. This directly explains why three right angles force the fourth to be 90° as well, closing the question raised at the outset.\n\nSection 4.3 reasons about parallelograms and then applies the deduced properties to find their sides and angles. The section begins by asking whether quadrilaterals with parallel opposite sides but non-right angles exist, and constructs one by drawing two non-perpendicular pairs of parallel lines, defining a parallelogram as a quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel. A Venn diagram places rectangles as a special subclass of parallelograms. Deduction 6 proves that adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to 180° (co-interior angles on parallel lines) and opposite angles are equal, using a general angle x to derive all four angles algebraically. Deduction 7 proves that opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal via AAS congruence on the two triangles formed by a diagonal. Deduction 8 proves that the diagonals bisect each other using ASA congruence on the two triangles formed at the intersection point, exploiting alternate angles from the parallel sides. The section lists four properties of parallelograms: opposite sides equal; opposite sides parallel; adjacent angles supplementary and opposite angles equal; diagonals bisect each other.\n\nSection 4.4 reasons about rhombuses — quadrilaterals with all sides equal — and deduces their angle and diagonal properties. The section constructs a rhombus by fixing two equal adjacent sides at an arbitrary angle and locating the fourth vertex by intersecting equal-radius arcs from the other two vertices, showing that such a figure exists for any non-straight angle. Deduction 9 proves that in any rhombus the diagonal divides it into two isosceles triangles whose base angles are all equal (four equal angles per diagonal), so opposite angles of the rhombus are equal and adjacent angles are supplementary. The argument further shows that opposite sides of a rhombus are parallel (alternate angles from the equal diagonal angles), establishing that every rhombus is a parallelogram — so all four parallelogram properties carry over. Deduction 10 proves that the diagonals of a rhombus intersect at 90°: SSS congruence of the two half-triangles at the intersection forces the two angles there to be equal and supplementary, hence each is 90°. Six properties of a rhombus are listed: all sides equal; opposite sides parallel; adjacent angles supplementary and opposite angles equal; diagonals bisect each other; diagonals bisect the corner angles; diagonals perpendicular.\n\nSection 4.5 applies the diagonal-construction principles studied so far through hands-on geoboard and triangle-joining activities. The Geoboard Activity asks students to place two rubber bands as perpendicular equal-length diagonals, identify the resulting quadrilateral, and then extend one diagonal by 2 cm on both sides and re-identify the shape, practising the link between diagonal properties and quadrilateral type. The Joining Triangles activity uses cardboard cutouts: two equilateral triangles joined along a common side produce a rhombus (to be justified); two isosceles triangles (8, 8, 6 cm sides) joined in two different orientations produce a rhombus or a kite (to be identified and justified); two scalene triangles (6, 9, 12 cm sides) joined in different ways produce various quadrilaterals for students to identify and justify. These activities consolidate the definitions and diagonal properties of parallelograms, rhombuses, and kites through construction and geometric reasoning.\n\nSection 4.6 recalls the definitions of kites and trapeziums and then reasons about their key properties. The kite is defined as a quadrilateral ABCD with AB = BC and CD = DA (two pairs of consecutive equal sides). Property 1 of the kite states that the diagonal BD bisects both vertex angles (∠ABC and ∠ADC) and is the perpendicular bisector of diagonal AC (AO = OC and BD ⊥ AC); students are prompted to justify this using congruent triangles (∆AOB ≅ ∆COB by SSS). The trapezium is defined as a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel opposite sides, and students are asked to construct one and find its remaining angles using co-interior angle properties (Property 1: ∠S + ∠P = 180° and ∠R + ∠Q = 180° for PQ ∥ SR). An isosceles trapezium — one whose non-parallel sides are equal — is then introduced; by dropping perpendiculars from the parallel side and showing the two corner triangles congruent (by RHS), Property 2 is derived: the base angles (angles opposite the equal sides) of an isosceles trapezium are equal.",

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 45-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 45 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

OUTPUT — exactly this JSON object, nothing else:
{
  "synthesis_unit": {
    "activity_title": "…",
    "pedagogical_method": "one of: Discovery · Problem-solving · Play-way · Inductive ·
      Deductive — the method this unit runs on",
    "section_goal": "recall | reason | apply — the goal this unit works at",
    "teacher_notes": "a few sentences: how the sitting runs, what to watch for, and the
      chapter method each problem needs — NOT the solutions, which are in the table",
    "visual_aids": [
      {"type": "table",
        "title": "Problems and solutions",
        "table": "No. | Problem | Solution\n1 | … | …\n2 | … | …"}
    ],
    "materials": ["…"],
    "time_bands": [
      {"minutes": "0-N", "activity": "…"},
      …bands in sequence, integer boundaries, last band ends at 45…
    ],
    "textbook_items_in_class": [],
    "homework": []
  }
}
No other keys — the platform carries the unit's number, duration, section coverage and
synthesis marker itself.
