CHAPTER SUMMARY:

{
  "stage": "middle",
  "subject": "mathematics",
  "grade": "viii",
  "chapter_number": 6,
  "chapter_title": "We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply",
  "sections": [
    {
      "ref": "section 6.1",
      "title": "Some Properties of Multiplication",
      "section_goal": ["recall", "apply"]
    },
    {
      "ref": "section 6.2",
      "title": "Special Cases of the Distributive Property",
      "section_goal": ["reason"]
    },
    {
      "ref": "section 6.3",
      "title": "Mind the Mistake, Mend the Mistake",
      "section_goal": ["apply"]
    },
    {
      "ref": "section 6.4",
      "title": "This Way or That Way, All Ways Lead to the Bay",
      "section_goal": ["reason"]
    }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 6.1 defines the distributive property of multiplication over addition — a(b+c) = ab+ac — and applies it systematically to reason about how products change when the numbers being multiplied are incremented or decremented. The section opens with an exploratory prompt about what happens to 23×27 when each factor is increased by 1, using this concrete case to motivate the general identity. Using distributivity, the chapter establishes that increasing b by 1 in the product ab increases the product by a; increasing both a and b by 1 increases the product by a+b+1. This is formalised as Identity 1: (a+m)(b+n) = ab+mb+an+mn, visualised through an area diagram partitioning a rectangle into four sub-regions. The section then shows that the same single identity handles all combinations of increase and decrease by treating decrements as addition of negative quantities. Three worked examples illustrate the mechanics: Example 1 expands a monomial over a three-term expression (3a/2)(a−b+1/5), introducing like-term collection and exponent notation; Example 2 derives (a+b)(a+b) = a²+2ab+b², noting the pairing of like terms ba and ab; Example 3 extends this to (a+b)(a²+2ab+b²) = a³+3a²b+3ab²+b³, demonstrating multi-step like-term collection. The second subsection shows how distributivity enables fast mental multiplication: multiplying a number by 11 is equivalent to shifting the number one place left and adding — reducing to digit-by-digit adjacent sums. Brahmagupta's khaṇḍa-guṇanam (multiplication by parts, Brahmasphuṭasiddhānta Verse 12.56) is cited as the earliest explicit statement of distributivity. The subsection extends the same logic to multiplication by 101, 1001, 10001 and to products such as 9734×99, all handled through the identity (a+m)(b+n).\n\nSection 6.2 derives and proves three special cases of Identity 1, grouping them under the heading of special products. The section reasons from geometry first: a square of sidelength (a+b) is partitioned into two smaller squares and two equal rectangles, yielding the visual justification of (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b² (Identity 1A). The same geometric argument is applied to (60−5)² to show that removing two rectangles and restoring one small square gives (a−b)² = a²−2ab+b² (Identity 1B). The section proves algebraically that (a+b)(a−b) = a²−b² (Identity 1C) by expanding via distributivity and cancelling the like terms ab and −ab. Pattern 1 demonstrates that 2(a²+b²) = (a+b)²+(a−b)², derived by adding the expanded forms of 1A and 1B, connecting numerical observations (e.g. 2(5²+6²) = 11²+1²) to their algebraic explanation. Pattern 2 observes that differences of squares of equally-spaced numbers factor as a product of their sum and difference — verified by expanding (a+b)(a−b) — and notes Sridharacharya's method of computing a² as (a+b)(a−b)+b² for fast squaring. Both patterns are shown to hold for all integers and fractions.\n\nSection 6.3 applies all the algebraic rules learned so far to a diagnostic task: twelve simplified expressions are presented, some correct and some containing errors such as misapplied distributivity (e.g. −3p(−5p+2q) simplified as p−2q), incorrect squaring of binomials (e.g. (5m+6n)² stated as 25m²+36n²), confused multiplication and addition of like terms, and spurious factoring (e.g. y+2(y+2) rewritten as (y+2)²). Students must identify each error, explain the likely misconception, and write the correct expression. This section consolidates procedural fluency with all three identities and the basic distributive rule.\n\nSection 6.4 presents a growing visual pattern of circles arranged in stepped rectangular arrays and asks students to count circles at each step. Four distinct algebraic methods each yield a different-looking expression — (k+1)²−1, k²+2k, k(k+1)+k, k(k+2) — and the section reasons that all four are equivalent by expanding each to k²+2k, illustrating that multiple algebraic representations can describe the same quantity. The same multi-method approach is applied to a square-tile border pattern and two area problems involving rectangles and squares. In the area problems, Tadang's method (total square minus four rectangles), Yusuf's method (inner square directly), and Aditya's method (doubling a half-region) each produce a different expression that proves equivalent upon expansion using Identities 1A, 1B, or 1C. The final Figure it Out consolidates all three identities through computational practice (computing 46², 397×403, 91², 43×45), multi-step products, algebraic expression identification, calendar diagonal-product patterns, and verification of number-theoretic claims using remainder arithmetic and consecutive-number identities.",

  "enumerated_worked_examples": [
    {
      "id": "WE-1",
      "source_section": "section 6.1",
      "book_ref": "Example 1, section 6.1 p.140",
      "description": "Expand (3a/2)(a − b + 1/5) using distributivity over three terms; collect like terms using exponent notation."
    },
    {
      "id": "WE-2",
      "source_section": "section 6.1",
      "book_ref": "Example 2, section 6.1 p.141",
      "description": "Expand (a+b)(a+b) by treating (a+b) as a single factor; collect like terms ba and ab to derive a²+2ab+b²."
    },

      "id": "WE-3",
      "source_section": "section 6.1",
      "book_ref": "Example 3, section 6.1 p.141",
      "description": "Expand (a+b)(a²+2ab+b²) using distributivity; collect like terms a²b+2a²b and ab²+2ab² to derive a³+3a²b+3ab²+b³."
    }
  ],

      "book_ref": "Figure it Out Q1, section 6.1 p.142",

    },

      "book_ref": "Figure it Out Q3, section 6.1 p.143",

      "book_ref": "Figure it Out Q4, section 6.1 p.143",

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 45-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 45 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

OUTPUT — exactly this JSON object, nothing else:
{
  "synthesis_unit": {
    "activity_title": "…",
    "pedagogical_method": "one of: Discovery · Problem-solving · Play-way · Inductive ·
      Deductive — the method this unit runs on",
    "section_goal": "recall | reason | apply — the goal this unit works at",
    "teacher_notes": "a few sentences: how the sitting runs, what to watch for, and the
      chapter method each problem needs — NOT the solutions, which are in the table",
    "visual_aids": [
      {"type": "table",
        "title": "Problems and solutions",
        "table": "No. | Problem | Solution\n1 | … | …\n2 | … | …"}
    ],
    "materials": ["…"],
    "time_bands": [
      {"minutes": "0-N", "activity": "…"},
      …bands in sequence, integer boundaries, last band ends at 45…
    ],
    "textbook_items_in_class": [],
    "homework": []
  }
}
No other keys — the platform carries the unit's number, duration, section coverage and
synthesis marker itself.

  "prose_summary": "Section 7.1 identifies the concept of proportional change by having students observe digital images of a tiger at different sizes. Images A, C, and D look similar while B and E appear distorted. Students discover through measurement that similarity arises when width and height change by the same multiplicative factor — not by a constant additive difference. This introduces the core idea that proportional relationships are multiplicative. Students reason through why subtracting the same amount from both dimensions does not preserve shape, grounding the intuition before any formal definition is given.\n\nSection 7.2 defines the ratio as the formal mathematical tool for representing proportional relationships. The ratio of width to height of image A is expressed as 60:40 and students learn that a ratio a:b means for every a units of the first quantity there are b units of the second. The section shows that ratios of images A, C, and D are proportional because multiplying both terms by the same factor produces the other ratio, and introduces the double-colon notation a:b::c:d to denote that two ratios are in proportion.\n\nSection 7.3 applies the procedure of simplifying ratios to their lowest terms by dividing both terms by their HCF. Students find that images A and D both reduce to 3:2, confirming proportionality, while images B (2:1) and E (1:1) do not match. The section establishes that two ratios are in proportion when their simplest forms are identical, giving students a reliable algorithmic check for proportionality.\n\nSection 7.4 develops problem-solving fluency with proportional reasoning through twelve worked examples and two student activities. Examples 1–3 practise identifying proportional ratios and solving simple context problems (lemonade sweetness, wall cement). Examples 4–7 extend to open-ended classroom problems (school teacher-student ratio, blackboard dimensions) and fractional factors. The Trairasika subsection introduces the ancient Indian Rule of Three — the pramana:phala::ichchha:ichchhaphala framework of Aryabhata — and derives cross multiplication (ad = bc) algebraically, giving students both the historical motivation and the algebraic proof. Examples 8–12 apply cross multiplication to speed-distance-time problems (mid-day meal rice, car travel, tea price comparison), reinforcing the importance of unit consistency and distinguishing between directly proportional and inversely proportional situations (Puneeth's speed-time problem is flagged as a non-example where the Rule of Three does not apply).\n\nSection 7.5 introduces the concept of dividing a whole quantity into parts in a given ratio — sharing, but not equally. Through a hands-on activity with counters, students explore dividing 12 objects in the ratio 3:1 by iterative dealing. The section then develops the general formula: to divide x in the ratio m:n, the two parts are m·x/(m+n) and n·x/(m+n). Examples 11 and 12 apply this to business profit sharing (Prashanti and Bhuvan's food cart) and mixture alteration (adding cement to a sand-cement mix to change the ratio), building both computational fluency and multi-step reasoning.\n\nSection 7.6 provides a reference table of unit conversions — length (metres to feet), area (square metres, acres, hectares), volume (mL to cc, litres), and temperature (Celsius to Fahrenheit) — needed for solving real-world proportional reasoning problems. The section does not develop new concepts but equips students to handle problems where quantities appear in different units before a proportion can be set up. A Figure it Out set of twelve problems integrates all prior skills with these conversions, covering contexts from planetary distances to ancient Lilavati problems, coin alloys, and farming manure quantities.",

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 45-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 45 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 45 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

  "prose_summary": "Section 2.1 explains, through geometric reasoning rooted in Baudhāyana's Śulba-Sūtra (c. 800 BCE), why the diagonal of a square produces a square of double the area. The section opens with Baudhāyana's question of how to construct a square with double the area of a given square, then reasons that simply doubling the side length produces a square four times as large. By drawing horizontal and vertical lines through the tilted square constructed on the diagonal, students see that the original square is composed of two small triangles while the new square is composed of four congruent triangles — establishing the doubling relationship. A hands-on paper-cutting activity reinforces this: two identical squares are each cut along their diagonals into four triangular pieces, and four of the triangles are arranged around an intact square to produce a square with double the area. The sequence can be extended further to produce squares of areas 2, 4, and 8 times an original, each being the square on the diagonal of the previous.\n\nSection 2.2 reasons through the reverse construction — halving a square — by drawing a tilted square inside a larger one whose vertices are the midpoints of the larger square's sides. The section justifies geometrically, using east-west and north-south auxiliary lines, why the inner square has exactly half the area of the outer square. A paper-folding activity directs students to fold a square inward so that crease lines pass through the midpoints of the sides, producing quadrilateral PQRS, and then to prove using diagonal properties and triangle congruence that PQRS is indeed a square with half the area.\n\nSection 2.3 defines the hypotenuse as the side opposite the right angle in a right triangle, then reasons from the doubling result to determine the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle with legs of length 1. Since the diagonal of a unit square has a square of area 2 constructed on it, the hypotenuse c satisfies c² = 2, giving c = √2. The section then applies this to find hypotenuses of isosceles right triangles with general equal-side length a via the formula c² = 2a², illustrating with worked examples (a = 12 giving c = √288, between 16 and 17; and c = √72 giving a = 6). The section also investigates the decimal nature of √2 through successive bounding — establishing 1 < √2 < 2, then 1.4 < √2 < 1.5, then 1.41 < √2 < 1.42, then 1.414 < √2 < 1.415 — and then proves by considering the last digit of terminating decimals and by prime factorization arguments that √2 can neither be expressed as a terminating decimal nor as a fraction m/n with m, n positive integers.\n\nSection 2.4 reasons through Baudhāyana's general solution (Śulba-Sūtra Verse 1.12) to combining two different-sized squares into a single larger square: form a right-angled triangle whose perpendicular sides equal the sides of the two smaller squares; the square on the hypotenuse has area equal to the sum of the two. Following Baudhāyana's Verse 2.1, the section constructs this result concretely by joining two different squares (sides a and b), marking a rectangular portion, drawing its diagonal to get a right triangle with legs a and b, and then placing four congruent copies of this right triangle to form a tilted four-sided figure over the hypotenuse. The section reasons that all four sides of this figure are equal (since all triangles are congruent) and all angles are right angles (using angle complementarity), establishing it as a square. The area identity — area of square on hypotenuse = sum of areas of original two squares — then follows directly, yielding Baudhāyana's Theorem: a² + b² = c². A paper-cutting activity has students cut two different-sized squares into three pieces and rearrange them into a larger square. The section also applies the theorem to the classical 3-4-5 example.\n\nSection 2.5 reasons about right-triangles with integer sidelengths (Baudhāyana triples). It introduces primitive and non-primitive triples, establishes by algebraic proof that if (a, b, c) is a Baudhāyana triple then (ka, kb, kc) is also one for any positive integer k, and uses the identity (n−1)² + (2n−1) = n² to generate primitive triples whenever 2n−1 is a perfect square (e.g., n=5 gives (3,4,5); n=13 gives (5,12,13)). The section thus shows there are infinitely many Baudhāyana triples and that every non-primitive triple is a scaled version of a primitive one.\n\nSection 2.6 recalls the history of Fermat's Last Theorem — inspired by the existence of infinitely many Baudhāyana triples, Fermat conjectured in the 17th century that xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ has no solution in positive integers for n > 2. The section recounts Fermat's famous marginal note claiming a proof he never wrote down, the 300+ years of failed attempts by great mathematicians, and Andrew Wiles's proof in 1994 after setting himself the goal as a 10-year-old in 1963.\n\nSection 2.7 applies the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem to a range of geometric problems. It opens with a classic problem from Bhāskarāchārya's Līlāvatī — a lotus stem of total length x+1 with tip 1 unit above water, whose tip touches the water 3 units away when bent — and solves it by setting up a right triangle of sides 3, x, x+1, giving x = 4 units depth. The section then applies the theorem to: finding the diagonal of a square, finding missing sides of right triangles from given dimensions, finding the side of a rhombus from its diagonals, and exploring grid-dot squares of various integer areas.",

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 45-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 45 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

OUTPUT — exactly this JSON object, nothing else:
{
  "synthesis_unit": {
    "activity_title": "…",
    "pedagogical_method": "one of: Discovery · Problem-solving · Play-way · Inductive ·
      Deductive — the method this unit runs on",

      chapter method each problem needs — NOT the solutions, which are in the table",

      {"type": "table",
        "title": "Problems and solutions",
        "table": "No. | Problem | Solution\n1 | … | …\n2 | … | …"}
    ],
    "materials": ["…"],
    "time_bands": [
      {"minutes": "0-N", "activity": "…"},
      …bands in sequence, integer boundaries, last band ends at 45…
    ],
    "textbook_items_in_class": [],

  }
}

  "prose_summary": "Section 3.1 recalls and identifies the core principle of proportional relationships: two ratios a:b and c:d are proportional if the cross-products are equal (a×d = b×c), or equivalently a/c = b/d. The idli batter example (Viswanath 6:3 vs Puneet 4:2) grounds the definition in a real-world cooking scenario and confirms both mixtures maintain the same 2:1 ratio, making the proportional relationship concrete before formal notation is introduced.\n\nSection 3.2 applies proportional reasoning to map scales. It defines the Representative Fraction (RF) as the ratio of map distance to actual ground distance, using RF 1:60,00,000 as the working example (1 cm on map equals 60 km on ground). Students use a ruler on a printed map of South India to measure distances between city pairs (Bengaluru–Chennai, Mangaluru–Chennai) and convert using the RF. A teacher-guided Map Making Activity directs students to sketch their own classroom to scale (1:50), placing furniture and fixtures at proportionally correct positions using appropriate symbols.\n\nSection 3.3 extends ratio notation beyond two terms and defines multi-term proportionality. Using a four-ingredient spice mix (coriander:chillies:dal:fenugreek :: 8:4:2:1), it shows how all terms scale by the same factor when quantities change proportionally. The general rule a/p = b/q = c/r = d/s formalises the relationship. Two worked examples apply multi-term ratios to mixing paint shades (Red:Blue:White :: 2:3:5, find red and blue for a given volume of white) and cement concrete (cement:sand:gravel :: 1:1.5:3, find total bags for 3 bags of cement).\n\nSection 3.4 solves for individual components when a whole quantity is divided in a given multi-term ratio. It extends the two-term division algorithm — divide the whole by the sum of ratio terms, then multiply each term — to three or more terms, stating the general formula: each part equals x × (its ratio term) / (sum of all ratio terms). Three worked examples cover finding component quantities in 110 units of concrete (ratio 1:1.5:3), finding ml of each paint colour for 50 ml of purple (ratio 2:3:5), and constructing a triangle whose angles are in ratio 1:3:5 (using the angle-sum constraint of 180°).\n\nSection 3.5 applies ratio-based division to pie chart construction. Starting from a grade-distribution table (A:B:C:D:E :: 12:10:8:6:4), it reduces the ratio to simplest form (6:5:4:3:2) using the HCF, then divides 360° proportionally to obtain sector angles (108°, 90°, 72°, 54°, 36°). A step-by-step construction procedure guides students to draw a circle, mark a radius, and measure successive angles with a protractor to complete and colour the pie chart. The section connects data visualisation directly back to the proportional division framework established in section 3.4.\n\nSection 3.6 defines inverse proportions and applies the relationship to a range of word problems. It begins by contrasting inverse with direct proportion: using a speed-time table (walk 5 km/h / 18h, bicycle 15/6, motorcycle 30/3, car 60/1.5), it shows that when one quantity increases by factor n, the other decreases by the same factor n, so their product xy = k (constant distance of 90 km). ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 45-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 45 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.

OUTPUT — exactly this JSON object, nothing else:
{
  "synthesis_unit": {
    "activity_title": "…",
    "pedagogical_method": "one of: Discovery · Problem-solving · Play-way · Inductive ·
      Deductive — the method this unit runs on",
    "section_goal": "recall | reason | apply — the goal this unit works at",
    "teacher_notes": "a few sentences: how the sitting runs, what to watch for, and the
      chapter method each problem needs — NOT the solutions, which are in the table",
    "visual_aids": [
      {"type": "table",
        "title": "Problems and solutions",
        "table": "No. | Problem | Solution\n1 | … | …\n2 | … | …"}
    ],
    "materials": ["…"],
    "time_bands": [
      {"minutes": "0-N", "activity": "…"},
      …bands in sequence, integer boundaries, last band ends at 45…
    ],
    "textbook_items_in_class": [],
    "homework": []
  }
}
No other keys — the platform carries the unit's number, duration, section coverage and
synthesis marker itself.

CHAPTER SUMMARY:

{
  "stage": "middle",
  "subject": "mathematics",
  "grade": "viii",
  "chapter_number": 12,
  "chapter_title": "Tales by Dots and Lines",
  "sections": [
    {
      "ref": "section 5.1",
      "title": "The Balancing Act",
      "section_goal": ["reason", "apply"]
    },
    {
      "ref": "section 5.2",
      "title": "Visualising and Interpreting Data",
      "section_goal": ["apply"]
    }
  ],
  "prose_summary": "Section 5.1 (The Balancing Act) reasons about the mean as a balance point and applies this insight to predict how mean and median shift when values are added, removed, or uniformly transformed. The section opens by revisiting mean as arithmetic average and reframes it geometrically: the mean is the unique point on a number line where the total distance of all values to its left equals the total distance to its right. Using dot plots, students verify this balance property for collections of two and three numbers and argue why the centre must be unique — shifting left or right immediately disturbs the equality of distances. The section then explores how the mean responds to adding or removing values: a value greater than the mean pulls it up, a value smaller pulls it down, and removing a value equal to the mean leaves it unchanged. Students investigate whether pairs or triples of values can be added or removed without changing the mean, discovering that symmetric additions around the current mean preserve balance. Next, the section proves algebraically what happens when every value in a dataset is increased or decreased by a fixed constant: the mean shifts by exactly that constant. A similar algebraic argument shows that multiplying every value by a constant scales the mean by the same factor, using the distributive property in both proofs. A parallel treatment covers the median: because the median is the middle value in sorted order, including a value larger than the current median increases it, while a value smaller decreases it. The section then moves to applied problem-solving: two worked problems (finding a smudged weight in a wrestler's record and correcting an over-counted coconut harvest) model how to use the mean formula to recover an unknown from a given average. The sub-section on mean and median with frequencies introduces frequency tables and shows that multiplying each value by its frequency before summing is necessary when data is not listed individually; it also shows how cumulative frequencies allow the median position to be located without writing out all values. The section closes with a spreadsheets sub-topic: students see how a digital spreadsheet is structured (rows, columns, cell references), learn to read a marks table, and learn to write SUM and AVERAGE formulae over row and column ranges, connecting the abstract concept of mean to a practical computational tool.\n\nSection 5.2 (Visualising and Interpreting Data) applies a two-step interpret-and-infer process to several real data visualisations, building skill in reading line graphs, infographics, and time-use strips. The section introduces line graphs as the appropriate choice when data evolves over time, contrasting them with the clustered bar graphs seen in earlier grades. Two worked examples are developed in depth: monthly maximum temperature data for Kerala and Punjab across 2023, and annual satellite-launch counts for India, China, Russia, and worldwide from 2012 to 2024. For each, students first identify what the graph shows (scale, units, colour/marker conventions, time range) and then infer patterns and comparisons — Punjab's wider temperature range versus Kerala's near-constant climate, or the sharp acceleration of worldwide launches after 2020 driven largely by USA. The rainfall line graph for six Indian coastal cities introduces the idea that monthly-average data is itself a derived quantity (averaged over multiple years), prompting discussion of what the data can and cannot tell us. The section then presents an infographic — a choropleth map comparing per-capita rice and wheat consumption across Indian states — illustrating how colour encoding can reveal geographic patterns not visible in a table, and probing what inferences are valid versus speculative. The activity-strip sub-section introduces a novel representation: a 48-box colour-coded strip where each box represents a 30-minute interval across one day, and five activities are distinguished by colour. Students read and decode three of Manoj's day-strips (Friday through Sunday), infer which day features a long movie outing, and then create their own strips. The section ends with the sleep-duration curve — a line graph of average daily sleep time from age 6 to 75 — illustrating that a graph with 80 closely spaced data points looks like a smooth curve, making a line graph more readable than 70 columns would be, and prompting students to notice that sleep time decreases through adolescence, bottoms out in mid-adulthood, and rises again after age 50.",

      "id": "A-1",
      "source_section": "section 5.1",
      "book_ref": "Try This, p.107",
      "description": "Students explain algebraically (and using fair-share interpretation) what happens to the average when a fixed number is subtracted from every value, and then investigate what happens when every value is doubled."
    },
    {
      "id": "A-2",
      "source_section": "section 5.2",
      "book_ref": "Try This, p.125",
      "description": "Students create their own 48-box activity strip for different days of the week, marking five activity types in 30-minute intervals, and compare their strip with an adult family member's strip."
    },
    {
      "id": "A-3",
      "source_section": "section 5.2",
      "book_ref": "Try This, p.131",
      "description": "Students read a line graph of moonrise and moonset times over a month, identify the dates of amavasya (new moon) and purnima (full moon), and note patterns."
    }
  ],
  "enumerated_worked_examples": [
    {
      "id": "WE-1",
      "source_section": "section 5.1",
      "book_ref": "Finding the Unknown (wrestlers), p.109",
      "description": "Given the mean weight of 10 wrestlers (39.2 kg) and 9 of the 10 weights, uses the mean formula to set up and solve a linear equation to find the missing weight (43 kg)."
    },
    {
      "id": "WE-2",
      "source_section": "section 5.1",
      "book_ref": "Finding the Unknown (coconuts), p.109",
      "description": "Given the average coconut harvest per tree (25.6) across 15 trees and the information that one tree's count was recorded 3 more than actual, recovers the total harvest and computes the corrected average (25.4)."
    },
    {
      "id": "WE-3",
      "source_section": "section 5.1",
      "book_ref": "Mean and Median with Frequencies (family size), p.110",
      "description": "Calculates mean and median of a frequency-table dataset of family sizes for 36 students, demonstrating the weighted-sum formula for mean and the cumulative-frequency method for locating the median position."
    },
    {
      "id": "WE-4",
      "source_section": "section 5.2",
      "book_ref": "Line Graphs — Temperature (Kerala and Punjab), p.116–118",
      "description": "Demonstrates the two-step identify-then-infer process on a clustered line graph of monthly maximum temperatures (2023), identifying scale, markers, and trends; inferring Punjab's higher variability versus Kerala's near-constant tropical climate."
    },
    {

      "source_section": "section 5.2",
      "book_ref": "Line Graphs — Space Launches, p.119–120",
      "description": "Applies the two-step process to a multi-series line graph of annual space-object launches (2012–2024) for USA, China, Russia, and worldwide; distinguishes valid inferences from invalid ones (e.g., cannot infer Nepal launched nothing, cannot read individual year counts precisely from the graph)."
    }

      "book_ref": "Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.113",

ARUVI — CLOSING SYNTHESIS RE-AUTHORING · MATHEMATICS · MIDDLE STAGE

You are re-writing ONE unit: the closing whole-chapter synthesis of a chapter's fullest
lesson plan. It is served in two situations and must be excellent in both:

1. As the FINAL unit of the fullest plan — the class finishes the chapter with it.
2. As ONE EXTRA 45-minute period appended to a SHORTER complete plan of the same
   chapter, whose own final unit (given below) already drew the chapter together
   yesterday.

THE UNIT YOU ARE WRITING closes the chapter by putting its methods to work on a small set
of problems the teacher poses. Solving them IS the synthesis: the chapter is drawn
together by being used, not by being recited.

PROPERTIES OF THE UNIT:
- It carries TWO TO FOUR problems, each reaching for a DIFFERENT major method of the
  chapter, and together spanning its main strands. Each problem is stated in full, with
  its numbers, inside the band that poses it — a teacher reads the band aloud and the
  class can start.
- The problems are the TEACHER'S OWN, written for this unit and posed on the board. The
  mathematics in each is the chapter's, and nothing is invented or imported.
- THE PROBLEMS AND THEIR SOLUTIONS LIVE IN ONE TABLE, in `visual_aids` — three columns,
  `No. | Problem | Solution`, one row per problem. The Problem cell states the problem in
  one or two plain sentences with its numbers. The Solution cell gives the answer and the
  few steps that reach it, in plain words and figures — brief enough for a teacher to read
  at a glance while the class works, and no longer than the problem it answers. This table
  is the teacher's whole worked reference.
- EACH PROBLEM IS WELL-POSED AND SELF-CONSISTENT. It states everything needed to solve it,
  its data agree with each other and with the solution beside it, and it has one answer.
  Where a count is named ("the four corner cells", "the six expressions you can form"),
  that count is the number the problem's own conditions produce. Where a figure carries
  measurements, they can all hold at once. Where a construction is described, the described
  construction is the one the solution works on.
- THE SOLUTION CELL IS THE SETTLED ANSWER. Work each problem out fully first; then write
  only the route that reaches the answer and the answer itself. Trials that failed,
  possibilities considered and rejected, re-checks and corrections belong to the working,
  not to the page a teacher reads at the board. Every step written is a step that holds:
  a justification names the fact it rests on, and never assumes what it is proving.
- `teacher_notes` is SHORT — a few sentences at most. It says how the sitting is run and
  what to watch for as students work; the mathematics is in the table, and is not repeated
  here. Name, for each problem, only the chapter method it needs — the method its own
  solution actually uses — and warn only about errors that problem can produce.
- Its `textbook_items_in_class` and `homework` are both `[]`, and its band text names no
  page, no exercise and no book item. The class works from the board.
- Its shape gives every student a full attempt before any answer is public: the problems
  are posed, worked individually with full working, compared in small groups where a
  disagreement is reconstructed step by step, and then presented — and each presentation
  is followed by the class NAMING the chapter method the solution rested on.
- The closing band states the chapter's one idea in a sentence, as the reason the problems
  yielded — earned closure, not ceremony.
- It is ONE sitting and weighs the same as any other: 45 minutes, a handful of
  bands, materials any classroom has. Depth here is the demand of the problems, never the
  quantity of material.
- Every method it calls on appears in EVERY unit-title map given below — the shorter plans
  differ in what they reach, so write only to what all of them share, and treat the
  SHORTEST map as binding.
- Its vehicle differs in kind from every FINAL UNIT given below, and it reuses none of
  their specific contexts, objects, puzzles or framing questions.
- Band narration never states a quantity of minutes and never points beyond this sitting —
  the band's `minutes` field carries the clock.
